Then we had the Mechanics Bank, of Montreal; the Bank of Liverpool, Liverpool, Nova Scotia; the Bank of Prince Edward Island, of Charlottetown; the Exchange Bank of Canada, of Montreal; the Maritime Bank of the Dominion of Canada, of St. John, N.B.; the Central Bank of Canada, of Toronto. This makes a total of seven banks. But there are three banks, La Banque du Peuple, La Banque de Saint-Jean and La Banque Ville-Marie, which were not alluded to by the hon. members of Laprairie, Rouville and St. Johns, and they are the only ones which were left unmentioned by those hon. members. What was the object of the gentlemen who passed over them in silence, and why did the newspapers supporting their party not allude, in their turn, to those three banks?

True it is that I mentioned La Banque Ville Marie, owing to the fact that it caused depositors in my county to sustain heavy losses; hut I did not do so because it was a French bank, for everybody knows that it was an English bank, having nothing of a French bank but the name.
Yes, but the majority of the depositors were French-Canadians.
That is true.

The strength of my argument remains unimpaired, and the hon. gentlemen must have had an object in view when they passed over the other banks in silence. I do not reproach them with having done so; they may think that this was fair means. But the people must know that a distinction was made, so that it might be said that under the Government of the great French-Canadian the French banks would have been made the

object of a better treatment. Fortunately, the facts shall be known, and those appeals smelling demagogism shall have no result. I shall not go so far as to say that such means was resorted to by members of this House, for everybody knows that there is not a Liberal member who would make appeals of that kind. The hon. member for Laprairie does not seem to approve what I am now stating. His' conscience may not happen to feel altogether at ease in this connection.
When you came to La-prairie in 1886 you were far from preaching the doctrine which you preach to-day.
You are far from the Farmers Bank, but if you wish to go back to the past, I am ready to follow you.
I am reminding you of 1886.

If my hon. friend
wishes to go as far 'back as 1886 he will know whom to speak to.
Now, there is a bank to which I desire to call the attention of the House, it is the Bank of Acadia. It does not bear a French-Canadian name, and it has a particular and an eloquent history. It lived just three months and twenty-six days, it re-opened its doors for a few days and redeemed for a few thousand dollars' worth of its notes. This lasted but a day or two and the rest of the people who were holding notes, with the exception of the Government, got nothing. The federal Government got twenty-five cents on the dollar out of many thousands of dollars which they had deposited.
Here is a bank which ought to be considered at least on the same footing as those mentioned by the Opposition. The question was not raised and it cannot be raised because the case is not the same. I think my hon. friends of the Opposition will admit with me that there is, from a certain standpoint, an enormous difference which is surely important to note, and it is this: The depositors of the Farmers Bank are entreating the Government, by means of petitions; delegations have come here again and again to explain their case and to ask for the justice which, to their mind, should be meted out to them. Up to this date, neither La Banque de Saint-Jean nor La Banque Ville-Marie nor La Banque du Peuple have taken the least step to show the Government that their depositors ought to be reimbursed. Will the Opposition claim that, in the absence of any request on the part of those depositors, the Government should have told them that they were to be reimbursed, and should have acknowledged their case as being fair and legitimate; that the Government, in short, should offer those depositors to reimburse them without a petition being made by them to that effect? Evidently no.
The depositors of the Farmers Bank, rightly or wrongly, have entreated us, through their lawyers and through numerous delegations, to reimburse they. They said: Here are the facts as we understand them, and they justify our request to the effect of being reimbursed. Considering those representations, should we not give the petitioners the benefit of the doubt? The other banks did not even make a request. Are we not forced, by the same process of reasoning, to the conclusion that if they made no request it was because they did not think they were entitled to reimbursement.
Let us proceed further. To those who, in the province of Quebec, would go and say that the depositors of La Banque de Saint-Jean, La Banque Ville Marie and La Banque du Peuple are not treated like the depositors of the Farmers Bank-and the hon. member for St. John has, in a very clever way, given to understand that any step would be useless, since, he said, the Minister of Finance had explicitly replied 'no' to the questions which he was asked-I shall answer that we have made an inquiry after refusing thus far to grant fhe request which was addressed to us, and that we are to-day taking action on the report of that inquiry.
Mr. Speaker, this Government does not propose to mete out a different treatment to the depositors of any bank which has become bankrupt, be it English or French or be they Protestants or Catholics. And if the same condition of things is evidenced in behalf of any other bank in the country, the same measure of justice shall be given to all concerned, no matter what province or nationality the depositors may belong to.
The depositors of La Banque de Saint-Jean did not get anything, so far, but we are informed by the receiver that they are to get from twenty to thirty cents on their deposits.
The depositors of La Banque du Peuple got 75J cents on the dollar, and the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie 17J cents.
The depositors of the Farmers Bank shall not get a cent out of the winding up; but this does not mean that the same principle should not apply in the case where

the depositors have received a partial reimbursement, as I have just said.
The case of the Farmers Bank is absolutely exceptional in the history of our banks, aside from the case of the Bank of Acadia, the depositors of which have not received a cent.- The Farmers Bank gets the treatment of justice involved' in the Bill now before the House. The case of the bank is not the same, and if it were true, iis is said in the Liberal papers of the -province of Quebec, that Toronto always gives the Government the word of command, we could have refunded to the depositors of the Bank of Acadia the meagre sum of $17,950-which was the total amount of the deposits made at that bank. If, as it is claimed, it is a principle to reimburse the English banks and to slight the French banks, it would have -been an easy thing to refund to the depositors of the Bank of Acadia such a Small sum, which was but a trifle owing to the High figure of our revenue.
The hon. member- for St. Johns said that La Banque de Saint-Jean should never have opened its doors. That bank has had thirty-three or thirty-four years of existence. I appeal to the spirit of justice of the hon. member. If he could throw off his political barnacles for a moment, would he not see that there is a difference to make between a bank the certificate of which jias just been issued or was issued two or three years ago and a bank which received its certificate in 1873, and has been in existence during thirty-four years. The case of the other banks is the same, or about the same, and the record of the Farmers Bank contains the report of facts unknown in the case of any of those other banks. However, if it can be -shown that there are exceptional facts in the ease of those banks-, the Government is ready to consider them with the sam-e spirit of justice and equity with which it did consider the facts relating to the ease of the Farmers Bank.
But what have we before us? Nothing has been submitted to the Government, so far. The hon. member alluded to the officials of the Finance Department and of the Treasury Board. He expatiated at length to establish that if those employees were at fault as regards the issuing of a certificate to the Farmers Bank, they ought to be dismissed. My hon. friend has committed an error, for those employees are not responsible, and it would not be fair to make them suffer on account of

this legislation, when the fact is that they are honest and respectable and have served faithfully under both Governments. It is not the officials of the Treasury Board or of the Finance Department who are at fault, it is the members of the former Administration who composed the Treasury Board. They -are the responsible parties, for it must be borne in mind that there is no official of the Finance Department at the service of the Treasury Board. This board is composed of "a certain number of ministers, and is called upon to examine and to -grant the certificate which the law requires, and no bank can begin to do business without having first obtained this certificate. The error in the case of the Farmers Bank was committed by the members of the former Administration who composed the Treasury Board.
Travers, the wretched man who is now suffering for his faults-I should say for his crimes-tried to make an immense speculation by means of the Bank Act. He came here and applied for the certificate required. The Minister of Finance, chairman of the Treasury Board, had been warned to the effect that this certificate should not be issued. That fact cannot be denied, although Mr. Fielding denied it before the House, and whatever assertions have been made by the hon. member for H-alton (Mr. Henderson) and by Sir Edmund Osier, of East Toronto. And Sir William Meredith, the commissioner appointed to hold an inquiry into this matter, had to come to the conclusion that he had faith in the evidence given before him to show that the ex-Minister of Finance had been warned. Moreover, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, one of the most distinguished lawyers in the land, had sent the Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, a letter to the effect that there was some fraud, and he added: Here is a duplicate of the judicial procedure by which it appears that Travers and the others are perpetrating an injustice and a fraud at the expense of the public. Considering those circumstances, considering the warnings of Mr. Osier and of Mr. Henderson, two members of this House, and the judicial documents transmitted by Mr. McCarthy, will anybody claim that Mr. Fielding should not have stopped and made an inquiry in order to ascertain as to whether those charges were well founded? Mr. Fielding himself admitted that he should have done so when he said, in view of his own justification, that it is very much easier to he a prophet after than

before the fact. He had to acknowledge that an error had been committed. That error has been acknowledged, and the report made by Judge Meredith testifies to that fact in indelible letters.
What was the result? The farmers of the neighbouring counties, depending upon the guarantee that the law gave them, depending upon the certificate issued, a certificate which is granted but after all the formalities have been complied with in the regular way; depending also upon the fact that the Treasury Board had opened the doors of that bank, said to themselves: The Farmers Bank has been incorporated by Parliament; the Treasury Board has examined everything and issued its certificate, but it did not make it known to us that it 'had been warned that there was error and fraud. Then the farmers went with the greatest security in the world and deposited their money at that bank. Can it be claimed to-day that bad management was the only cause of the failure of that bank? Bad management was but a link of the chain wrought by Mr. Fielding the day he gave his authorization.
If those farmers had been told that the certificate was granted, but that Mr. McCarthy had warned the minister that there was fraud, do you think they would have fetched their money to that bank? It is true that Mr. McCarthy withdrew his opposition afterwards, because owing to the proceedings taken, his clients were disinterested. But were there not facts serious enough to open the eyes of Mr. Fielding?
Upon being made aware of the judicial proceedings, Travers hastened to reimburse Mr. McCarthy's clients, because he had succeeded in shearing other sheep. Why did Mr. Fielding fail to say that to the public? If the farmers of Ontario had known what Mr. Fielding did know, who will claim that any one of them would have deposited a dollar at that bank?
Sir Edward Clouston, manager of the Bank of Montreal, president of the Bankers' Association, wrote Mr. Fielding: You have made an error, and you should withdraw this certificate at once. Did Mr. Fielding, after he was supplied with this warning, take the least step to cancel the certificate and put the public on their guard)? No. And I call the attention of the House to the fact that even if Mr. Fielding had not succeeded in withdrawing this certificate, there was a proceeding provided by the law; the Minister of
Justice in his capacity as Attorney General of Canada could have taken at once a writ of privilege to have the certificate cancelled. My hon. friends from Rouville and St, Johns know that proceeding and they will say nothing to the contrary. I assert that one can plead error on the issuing of the certificate, and every one will admit that. I claim that a politician who committed an error of that kind must acknowledge it and try to redress it, and if this had been done, $1,200,000 would not have been absorbed by the thefts and fraudulent speculations of Travers.
We are told to-day that the collapse of this bank was due to bad management and to frauds committed by Travers. I have no hesitation in saying that the former Administration led those people into error by granting the certificate-although I do not deny that they may have acted in good faith-and that those same people lost their money for that reason. And we would be told that the Government is not doing its solemn duty by reimbursing them? One cannot have it admitted that the Government is not acting correctly in this matter and in such a way as to deserve the hearty and entire support of both sides of this House.
Taking the circumstances into consideration, I understand how repugnant it is for the hon. gentlemen to the left to vote in favour of this measure, as the error in question was made by the Minister of Finance of their own Government. iSuch a vote would be tantamount to scourging their own minister. But the least I can say is that they should not come and charge this Government with doling something immoral, because it is trying to redress the error in question. By taking in the treasury the amount which is necessary to reimburse those who have sustained losses originating from the fault of the Government we are Tendering to Ceasar what is due to 'Caesar and to the farmers what is due to the farmers. Whatever may be the charges made against us, we are satisfied that we are fulfilling a duty which may be disagreeable, but which is at the same time, an imperative duty. Surely, there is nothing agreeable in taking over a million dollars to reimburse the depositors of a certain bank, when we have so many other needs for which we could make use of this money. But when a country has a revenue of $175,000,000 to $200,000,000, it would look very bad on their part to indulge in parsimony and refuse to redress a

grievance resulting from an error because false charges were dreaded. We have risen above such considerations, and the same measure of justice will be meted out to those to whom justice is 'due.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has displayed so much warmth during his special plea that I expect he has a very bad case-and it is a bad case indeed. I approve unreservedly the statement made by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) that this is an immoral piece of legislation. The Postmaster General stated a moment ago that this was the view taken by the Liberal party in this House because, forsooth, the Liberal party could not stand to repair an injustice committed by the late Minister of Finance, Hon. William Stevens Fielding. Let me quote from the book of books, from the most respectable Conservative paper in the land, the Montreal Gazette, published, one might say, at the very threshold of the biggest financial institution of the country, the Bank of Montreal; inspired in its financial columns by the best minds of the country. Let me read the opinion of the Montreal Gazette on this piece of legislation. On Tnursday, May 28, the Montreal Gazette said:
The demand in the case of the Quebec banks named is based on the action promised for the relief of the losers by the collapse of the Farmers Bank of Toronto. The unwisdom of such action was shown when it was first suggested. The present position only makes it more plain. It foreshadows a situation in which the Government and Parliament will be called upon to make good the losses of every failed bank. Indeed, some have regarded the action with complacency as the beginning of a Government guarantee of bank deposits, a thing that would encourage every reckless man in charge of a bank and make the national treasury a reserve fund for the incapable to draw upon for their natural losses. There is one reply that the Government can make to those who are seeking compensation for their business losses through the failure of banks in this province. It can only be made effectively and so as to cause the ministers and their party no harm after the proposal to pay the losses of Farmers Bank depositors has been abandoned. The proposal that Parliament shall vote money in aid of the Farmers Bank creditors has hurt the Government with the business community To press the measure-
Even in this House, and we all know that it will be killed by the Senate and by Conservative Senators.
To press the measure will hurt it further wherever there is a man who has lost through the failure of other banks and who will feel that he is being discriminated against. And, even in the face of a weakened opposition,

the Government is not in a position to invite hurt throughout the country for the sake of a few men-
Is the Minister of Labour in his seat? Yes, he is.
-who made unwise pledges during an election and then organized a raid to force their fulfilment.
Thus in a few terse sentences the Gazette has put the case as plainly as it can be put before the people of this country. This is obnoxious legislation and it invites reprisals. My hon. friend stated a moment ago that we on this side, the members who represent constituencies in Quebec, would ot fail in future to draw a comparison between the attitude of the Minister of Finance with respect to banks that have failed in Ontario and banks that have failed in Quebec. My hon. friend stated that we wanted to arouse the prejudices of our electors. But let me tell my hon. friend that the Banque Ville Marie, to which I shall refer in a moment, was an English bank with a French name. Therefore it is not a question of nationality and my hon. friend is enough of a business man to know that money has no nationality and deposits no sentiment. Let me refer my hon. friend to the language used in this House, not by a member belonging to the Liberal party but by an lion, gentleman who represents the Conservative traditions of the old city of Kingston, I refer to my friend Mr. Nickle. He was the first one who was generous and broad minded enough a few days ago to appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and to tell him that if he reimbursed the depositors of banks that have failed in one province he should have the courage to also reimburse the depositors of banks that have failed in other provinces. What did he say? On May the 11th my hon. friend from Kingston said:
Then we are running Into another difficulty. If recklessness and fraud were the efficient cause that led to the failure of this bank, I cannot see how we can make a distinction between a French-Canadian bank and an Ontario bank. What is law for Ontario-
Sir, the question of province was not raised by any of the French-Canadian members of this House, but it was raised very	generously by the hon. gentleman
who	represents Kingston (Mr. Nickle).
The reimbursement of the depositors in the case of La Banque de Saint-Jean, in the case of La Banque Ville Marie is not claimed as a matter of right because reimbursement of the depositors by the national treasury is not provided for in

the Bank Act. We all know that, it is the a b c of banking. But we say that if that principle is admitted in one case it should be also admitted in other cases, that if you discriminate in the case of the Farmers Bank you should extend that discrimination to the poor depositors of the Ville Marie Bank of the Bank of Saint-Jean; to my electors and the electors represented by the member for St. Johns and Iberville. I placed on the Order Paper a question with reference to the banks of our province and my hon. friend the Postmaster General finds fault with that. Why, he said you should have also mentioned all the banks that have failed in this country. I, Sir, do not represent the whole country. I represent nay electors from Rouville and from one parish alone, the parish of Marieville. 1 received petitions the other day with over one hundred signatures of depositors of the defunct Ville Marie Bank. I stand first for my electors; the hon. member for St. Johns stands first for his electors. And if the Government will undertake to say that in future the Government will reimburse depositors of other 'banks that have failed, I will stand for that principle not only for the depositors who have lost in my county but for the defrauded depositors all over the country as well.
Is that a fair statement of the case?

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance does not intend to apply that principal equally to all the provinces and to the banks of the various provinces. I charge him with having stated in this House that he intended to deliberately discriminate in favour of the Farmers Bank. On the 4th of May I asked:
Is it the intention of the Government to reimburse the depositors of the Ville Marie Bank, the Bank of St. Jean and the Banque du Peuple?
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance answered plainly and bluntly: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I ask my hon. friend on what ground.
On what ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I shall prove to my hon. friend at once that if there is one scintilla of reason and justification to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank, there is the same justification to reimburse the depositors of the Bank Ville Marie. I will
come to that point presently. I have here letters addressed during many years from 1892 until 1900, to the Minister of Finance by the Deputy Minister of Finance. They constitute the evidence that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he was Minister of Finance of this country knew that the Ville marie Bank was a rotten institution, and I will show my hon. friend that if-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What year was the Bank Ville Marie incorporated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
that the ground of this legislation is that the certificate of the Treasury Board should not have been issued to this bank.

Such ground does not
exist.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This bank should never
have been allowed to remain in business.

Or the other bank either, and I shall establish it to the satisfaction of my hon. friend. I shall come to that in a moment. I say that this legislation is immoral because it serves only mean political motives and nothing else. The hon. gentleman cannot find a banker of repute in Canada who will approve of this legislation. I would have cited to him the name of Sir Edward Clouston, but unfortunately he has passed away. But his immediate successor, Mr. Angus, would not approve of this. Take the president of the Bank of Montreal, take the president of the Bank of Commerce and if my hon. friend can show this House that he approves of this legislation I shall vote for this Bill now before the House. I say not one banker of repute in the country favours this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my non. friend think this House should be bound by the opinion of any individual man?

That is a very lame answer on the part of an able gentleman like the Minister of Finance. I shall go further. We have not yet heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I hope we shall hear from him before this debate is over. I believe in my soul and conscience, that had he occupied the position of my hon. friend on the Treasury benches he would never have promoted this mischievous legislation. I say it and I believe

it. Sir, this is a populist piece of legislation. *We have not reached in Canada that point where just to cater to a little popularity in a few constituencies Parliament will trample upon the banking and the 'business traditions of the country. I repeat, let my hon. friend take the opinion of Sir Edmund Byron Walker, that of Sir Frederick Taylor of the Bank of Montreal, of the president of the Royal Bank of Canada and if they favour this legislation I shall accept their verdict. Not only that, but I say that the very motive which animates the hon. gentlemen in promoting this legislation is an unworthy one. It is evident that this $1,200,000 is only a tip paid to the electors of a few constituencies who were promised at the last general election that if they supported the Tory party they would get this reimbursement. Let me read quietly, while the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in this House, the petition which was sent to this Government a few months after they reached office :
At this meeting of depositors of the Farmers Bank of Canada at Pontypool, assembled, upon a motion of Mr. Thomas Hill and seconded by Mr. Geo. Douglas, it is hereby unanimously resolved after hearing read the speeches made in Parliament in March, 1911, on the Farmers Bank question by the Bight Hon. R. L. Borden, Hon. Messrs. Foster, Crothers and Hughes, and by Messrs. Armstrong, Blain, Beattie, Boyce, Donnelly, Henderson, Edwards, Porter, North-rup, Sharpe, Thornton and Taylor and others, and as in the election which was held in September last the Conservative party continued to take the attitude assumed by them in Parliament in the previous March;
And whereas promises were made that justice would be done the depositors in the event of the Conservative party being elected;
And whereas literature was circulated during the election on behalf of the Conservative party ;
And whereas the Conservative party was returned to power, the public being fully cognizant of its attitude upon the Farmers Bank question, and as nothing appears to havo been done up to the present time by the Conservative party:
Now, therefore, this meeting assembled hereby respectfully requests the Government of this country to carry out the policy on this question, upon which they were returned to power.
It is hereby requested that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Right Hon. R. L. Borden, and to the hon. Minister of Finance, and to C. J. Thornton, Esq., M.P.
(Sgd) M. H. Minore,
Chairman.
There we have the origin, the causa causans of this legislation. My hon. friend, so long as he speaks in English, and he speaks it beautifully, captivates and captures. But beware of him when he speaks Latin! He spoke yesterday of the causa causans. It is fine casuistry.

Last night my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was distinguishing between the efficient cause and the other causes, and he told my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) that he should know what is in law the causa causans. Well, I hold in my hand the causa causans, and it is the petition forwarded by the Ontario voters just after the last election and mentioning the pledges given by the Conservative members to their constituents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quote what the commissioner said.

Here is what the commissioner said:
Notwithstanding the irregularities on the part of Travers and his misconduct in connection with the application for the certificate, which I have mentioned, the evidence satisfies me that if the bank had been prudently and honestly managed there is no reason why it should not have succeeded. The promissory notes that had been given by subscribers were for the most part good and were subsequently paid, and while it is true that if the certificate of the Treasury Board had not been granted the money of the shareholders and depositors would not have been lost, the efficient cause of that loss was the recklessness and fraud of those entrusted with the management of the bank, and not the granting of the certificate.
The Postmaster General stated a moment ago that he was very sorry that Mr. Fielding was morally responsible for the failure of the bank; it was, he said, the certificate which he granted which was the invitation to so many depositors, and the first dollar deposited in that bank was deposited there because indeed Mr. Fielding bad issued the certificate. Well, it is just six o'clock, but let me tell the hon. gentleman that the farmers who deposited their money in the bank did so, not because of the certificate, but because Mr. Beattie Nesbitt, the Tory boss of Toronto, was running the whole business and doing the advertising.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, just before recess I was explaining to the House that this legislation was in my judgment, and in the judgment of unbiased people in the community, immoral, obnoxious and insidious, and if it is adopted-I hope it will never be-it will invite for the future other raids on the treasury of Canada. The duty of a minister of finance was well defined to-day by the Minister of Labour. Certainly, the Minister of Finance is the

trustee of the moneys of the people, and therefore the paramount duty of the Minister of Finance is above all to resist raids on the treasury. I said before dinner that this legislation smacks of populism, and it does. The Minister of Finance should never forget that he is the Hon. Thomas White, Minister of Finance of Canada, and that he should not leave himself open to be compared with General Coxey leading his band of raiders on the Washington treasury. The hon. gentleman should never forget that this is Ottawa, the capital city of the brightest of the overseas dominions, the Washington of the North as it has been called by D'Arcy McGee and Sir Wilfrid Laurier; this is Ottawa, but the Minister of Finance seems to think it is Oklahoma. The Minister of Finance although well-built and of magnificent stature is singularly weak; he lacks firmness and resolution, and I will explain wdiy. It is because with his undoubted ability, and his standing, he has joined the Conservative party at the eleventh hour, and having reached the summit in one gigantic stride he must do something to be forgiven his rapid ascendancy in the ranks of that party. That is why he has yielded on many occasions and that is why he yields now to the clamours of the raiders. The Minister of Finance must not forget that in his exalted position he is a leader and not a follower of men. I know he is a bookworm, and I wonder if he ever Tead Balzac's work where one of the characters said: je suis leur chef done je les suis. (I 'am their leader, therefore I follow them.)
It is admitted that in the political game, in the heat of a political campaign wild promises are often made. If I had to redeem all the promissory notes that have been signed during the last campaign, by the gentlemen I see in front of me just now, it would take the very treasury of Canada. In the heat of a general election, I say, wild promises are made, but the Government and especially the Minister of Finance is certainly not obliged to redeem all of the unscrupulous pledges. After having read the petition sent to the Government by the Tories of Ontario after the last election, I say that this legislation is the result of a political compact made during that campaign. It is playing the political game at the expense of the treasury. See how well it has been staged-it was a political game from the inception of this movement in order to seduce
the fifteen or sixteen constituents involved, and it still savours of a political game. Yes, see how well it has been staged; first a wild promise was made during the heat of the campaign in 1911; in 1912 not a word was uttered in this House in favour of the depositors; in 1913 the session passed and we heard nothing of it except in the dying days of the session a mild and vague promise made by the right hon. the Prime Minister. But we reach the year of our Lord 1914, in the month of June, in the dying days of this protracted session, just before another political campaign in the province of Ontario, and suddenly here comes the legislation which will secure the votes of the constituencies involved in the Farmers Bank. We are unfortunately accustomed to that game on the part the hon. gentlemen who sit on the Treasury benches. What happens to-day for the Farmers Bank on the eve of a provincial election in Ontario happened last year when the provincial election took place in Saskatchewan. We then saw something which had never been dreamt of in the annals of this country before; we saw the Government, by Order in Council, cutting the duty on cement by one-half in order to seduce the electors of that province, and immediately after the election these duties were put up to where they were before. In Chateauguay, in the month of October last, three or four days before the bye election, the parish of Chateauguay was bribed with a sum of $3,638.84.
This money was distributed amongst twenty-five or thirty electors just on the eve of an election in order to seduce the electors.

Will my hon. friend
* excuse me, because he is making a statement which he must know is absolutely incorrect? While a certain amount of money was spent in Chateauguay basin, it was spent in fulfilment of a promise made by the late Government, who deceived the people for years by not carrying out their pledges.

I thank my hon. friend for this admission. It is true that the late member for Chateauguay had promised certain works on the river Chateauguay, but he did not ask the Government to spend that money in the turmoil of a general election. The general election passed; but when the by-election came along, my hon. friend dipped into the treasury and took out nearly $4,000, which he spent as follows:

Jean Baptiste Chevreflls, foreman, period of employment, September 22 to December 31, $308.
That is one elector.
What was the date of the election?

I forget the exact date; but it was at the beginning of October.
Moi'se Durangeau, labourer, September 24 to November 19, $89.07 ; JSrSmie Lussier, labourer, September 24 to December 31, $96.63.
And I have a long list. I could name the whole parish. The money was spent just at the time when the election was being carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When was the money voted?
I do not think the money was even voted. The money was taken out of the general appropriations of the Department of Public Works-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then it must have been voted.	,

-and it was spent after a delegation from the county of Chateau-guay had approached my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works two weeks before the election. I have the thing very vividly in my memory. My hon. friend was at the Ritz Carlton hotel, where the delegation approached him. He is much more a leader in our province than the three representatives of the province of Quebec.

They are proud of
him.

And he is not proud of you. This delegation came to my hon. friend and made the application for that money during the election; and he told them: Certainly, if it is the wish of the people of Chateauguay, of course, you will get the money. They got the money, and the Conservatives carried the election.
I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to do me any injustice.
No.

I do not believe I ever
met a representative from the constituency of Chateauguay at the Ritz Carlton in my life.
Was it at the Windsor?
No.
Was it at the Conservative headquarters?
Perhaps it was.

I say that this is nothing less than corruption of the worst kind. In the case of the Farmers Bank, in the case of the reduction of duties just on the eve t,'f the election ir Saskatchewan, as in the minor case of the Chateauguay by-election, it is corruption and nothing else. And when my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) says that this is immoral legislation, he is stating the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
My hon. friend says that an error of judgment was made, and the commissioner has found that the Hon. Mr. Fielding unfortunately made that error of judgment. You, Sir, as an old member of the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada, will remember when, in the eighties, the Government of Sir John A. Malcdonald subsidized the famous enterprise known as the Chignecto Marine railway in the Maritime provinces. It was subsidized and I think even the bonds were guaranteed by the Government, although I am not sure as to that point.
No.

A company was formed in London. The capital was subscribed; the work was started, and suddenly the Government withdrew their subsidies from the company. Since that time, like the ghost of Banquo, we see in the lobbies of this House every year Mr. Provand. My hon. friend knows him. We have mqt him for the last fifteen years.
He is here yet.

He represents the old
company; and he insists now, as he has insisted for fifteen or sixteen years, on obtaining from the Government of Canada a reimbursement, the payment of a debt of honour, recognized as such by Sir Charles Tupper, for instance, and by other ministers. Has my hon. friend ever yielded to the clamour of the English capitalists who lost their money in that enterprise, guaranteed toy the Government of Canada?
Let us take the case of La Banque Internationale. The Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance-I will not say ' had refused,' because I know my hon. friend would quibble again-had declined to issue a certificate for good and valid reasons, which were stated in the document which my hon. friend found when after the 21st of September, 1911, he was sworn as Minister of Finance of Canada. What happened? In

spite of that Tefusal on the part of the Hon. Mr. Fielding to issue that certificate for good and valid reasons, six days after my hon. friend had been in office, he issued a certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Hon. Mr. Fielding did not refuse to issue the certificate.

I thought my hon.
friend would quibble again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He said that, in view of
the fact that there was a change of government, without passing any opinion upon the merits of the application, it should be left for the consideration of the incoming Administration. My hon. friend will find the minutes from the Treasury Board in the answer to a question which I handed in this morning. It is not true to say that Mr. Fielding refused the application of the bank.

My hon. friend is very unfortunate. I have the document with me, and I will give my hon. friend the reasons why Mr. Fielding declined to issue this certificate:
The board having submitted to them the further papers in connection with the application of La Banque Internationale for a certificate under the provisions of the Bank Act to enable it to commence business, is of the opinion that the matter requires more consideration than can be given to it in the present state of affairs, when a change of administration is about to take place.
Hear, hear.

Have patience. Do not give your hear, hears now.
The board, therefore, without expressing- any opinion on the merit of the application, desire to leave the papers for the consideration of the new Treasury Board.
Hear, hear.

But that is not all.
In taking this course it is desirable to state that apart from and in addition to the questions usually engaging the attention of the board in connection with an application for the granting of a certificate to a new bank to enable it to commence business, there are some matters which call for special consideration in connection with the present application.
Notice was served on the hon. gentleman to be very careful; there were special reasons for him to pause and to ponder before issuing the certificate. There is another feature.
While the amount of capital subscribed is much greater than the amount of subscribed capital in connection with any preceding application to the board, it also appears that, out of the total allotments of stock amounting to $9,239,400 made by the provincial directors, $7,156,000 thereof has been allotted to subscribers residing and domiciled in a foreign country. The amount of stock allotted to subscribers domiciled in Canada is $2,083,400. Foreign subscribers number 191; subscribers in Canada number 183.
The large amount and large proportion of . capital subscribed abroad in its relation to the provisions of the Bank Act, with regard to the enforcement of the double liability, is one of the matters referred to.
Still another feature, still another reason to specially consider whether the application should be granted.
There is another feature connected with the foreign subscriptions to which attention may here be drawn. One of these subscriptions is for 10,000 shares-$1,000,000 of the capital stock. The subscription is made in 1 trust.' The person or persons for whom the trust is held are not disclosed. In the absence of such disclosure the subscriber for this large amount, apparently in ordinary financial circumtsances (being in charge of the Paris office of Mr. R. Forget, the president of the bank), is alone responsible, so far as the records of the bank afford information as to persons liable, for the double liability should occasion arise for enforcing the provisions of the Act in regard thereto. There is a further subscription of $250,000 by the wife of the same party.
Here-are the additional reasons given in that document whether special consideration should be given to that application.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me to ask him a few questions ? Does he know any provision of the Bank Act under which foreign subscriptions are barred ? That is the first question. The second is: Is he not aware that, after all the foreign subscriptions are excluded, there were sufficient subscriptions of Canadian subscribers to comply with the requirements of the Bank Act ? And, further, does he know that instead of $250,000 required to be paid up by the Bank Act, a sum of nearly $1,000,000 was paid up in connection with La Banque Internationale ? And does he know, as a matter of fact, that in the case of no certificate ever issued to a bank in Canada were the provisions more strictly complied with and more amply fulfilled than in the case of this bank ?

That only confirms what I have already said about the Farmers Bank, that Mr. Fielding took every precaution which a man of judgment could take in the circumstances. If. on the other hand my hon. friend had paused for a moment when he reached the Treasury Benches, six days after he had been sworn in as minister, and

asked Mr. Fielding: How is it that you have left that document at the Treasury Board; axe there reasons why you doubt the validity of the stock which has been subscribed?-perhaps my hon. friend would have learned that at that moment it was known on the street that there was a pooling arrangement by which Canadian subscribers to the stock would not be called upon to pay more than ten per cent, but that European subscribers would pay one hundred per cent. I quoted that pooling arrangement in the House last year, and it was well known at the time my hon. friend issued the certificate. It would not have been wrong for him to have called on Mr. Fielding; he could have said to him: Mr. Fielding, you are no longer Minister of Finance it is true, but I have enough confidence in your loyalty to put some questions to you before I put my imprimatur on this certificate; why did you refuse to issue this certificate, because it is a serious matter to refuse this when apparently all of the procedure has been complied with? Here is, Sir, the pooling arrangement:
Whereas it has been deemed advisable to form a syndicate for the resale in a. proper and suitable manner of the shares of the Banque Internationale du Canada held by the shareholders of said bank who wish at a later date to dispose of all or part of their holdings. Whereas it is imperative that such operation be conducted by a manager of experience. Now, therefore, agreement witnesseth:
1.	The shareholder agrees to be a member of the syndicate formed by the present for the resale of the shares of the Banque Internationale du Canada now standing in his name.
2.	Those shares will stand pooled for the purpose of said syndicate for an irrevocable period of eighteen months.
3.	The manager will have the right and will use it in his own discretion to dispose of the pooled shares,-
Which is a huge speculation-

in all or in part at any time during the above-named period, to the best interest of the shareholders providing that a net profit of at least ten dollars a share be obtained for said shareholders.
4.	The manager will render account to the shareholders from time to time of the sales made for the syndicate account and same shall always be made pro rata to the shares of all shareholders.
5.	Any shareholders will have the privilege at any time to withdraw from sale the part of his shares which would not have then been disposed of, but said part of his shares will stand pooled until the liquidation of the syndicate and shall not be sold or disposed of by said shareholder during the life of the syndicate under penalty of having his shares forfeited for the benefit of the members of the syndicate.

Now comes the important paragraph:
6.	The manager binds and obliges himself during the life of this agreement to advance in the name and for the account of the members of the syndicate all and every call, except the first one already paid, which might be made by the Banque Internationale du Canada on the shares pooled in virtue of the present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is the agreement illegal or unlawful and a contravention of the Bank
Act?

Without having the Bank Act under my hand, I say this was an immoral agreement, because it was transforming a legitimate banking organization with foreigners-which is still worse the majority of the capital coming from France-into a gambling speculation. Air. Speaker, I do not say that my hon. friend is guilty. In that case he made an error of judgment. Is he responsible? Shall we hold him and the Government responsible for the lose sustained by the French and the Canadian investors? Does my hon. friend know that a million dollars which was paid up was reduced to $500,000, and that to-day the name of Canada in France, one of the great lending nations of the world, is blemished? Does he not know that, since that time, no one in France will invest money in Canada? However, I am pleased to say that my hon. friend is not guilty. He made an error of judgment. If he had paused a little and consulted Mr. Fielding, La Banque Internationale would never have been organized, $500,000 would never have been lost by the subscribers to the stock in that bank, and the name of Canada would never have been besmirched. I say that errors of judgment are made even by my hon. friend; were made even by great financiers like Sir Charles Tupper and Sir -Leonard Tilley in the case of the Chignecto Alarine Railway. Sir, at the opening of the session I brought to the attention of the House the case of one Fatsari, in respect of whom a judicial error was made by one of the judges in the province of Quebec whereby that poor Italian was convicted for manslaughter and sent to penitentiary for fifteen years. Five years afterwards the judge who had convicted him discovered his error, reported to the Minister of Justice, and Fatsari was released on the eve of Christmas. Fatsari's only consolation was the partaking of his Christmas dinner in the police station at Montreal with the policeman who had arrested him five years before. He had no roof to re-

ceive him; no family to welcome him. Sir, the Government of Canada, who appointed that judge, was responsible for that conviction. The logic of the hon. gentleman is: no certificate, no bank; no bank, no failure; no failure, no reimbursement. I say: no government, no judge; no judge, no judicial error; no judicial error, no penitentiary. My hon. friend has too much common sense and ability to countenance such logic.

Did the hon. member for Rouville not bring to the attention of this House the unfortunate case of the Italian whom he mentioned and ask this House if they would not do something for him because of an error of judgment?

Certainly. According to the logic of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, any act of negligence in this country can be traced to the door of the Cabinet. Take the case of an accident on the river St. Lawrence. The pilotage system is under the benevolent eye of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Three accidents have taken place in the river St. Lawrence since the opening of navigation, due in two cases to the pilot. The companies have suffered heavy damages; they have been obliged to put their steamers in the docks at Montreal for repairs. The pilots cannot pay, but the Government can pay, and, accepting the logic of my hon. friend in respect of the Farmers Bank, any company could come to my genial friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and say: you buoy the river St. Lawrence; you appoint the pilots; the pilotage system is under your control; an accident happened because the pilot did not do his duty, because he was drunk or because he was blind; therefore you should reimburse the company the damages they have suffered.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend would have to have them go to the pilot corporation; they control the qualification of pilots.

The pilot corporation
controls only the moneys with which the pilots are paid; they do not pay damages. Take the case of a registered letter. Suppose my hon. friend the Postmaster General, who is a prodigal, sends a registered letter to his brother or to a friend in Quebec county, containing $50 or $100. The money disappears because one of his letter carriers pilfered the letter. What recourse has the addressor against the letter carrier? He can send him to penitentiary for three years, but if he warts to get his
money back will the Postmaster General tell his deputy to refund him the money? Certainly he cannot do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is he supposed to
have had any notice of the dishonesty of the post office carrier?

I can tell my hon. friend that since September 21, 1911. all sorts of letter carriers have been appointed and the complaint in Montreal, Winnipeg, Quebec, Toronto and other large cities is that many letters disappear. But the point I wish to make is that the Government is not obliged to recoup the addressor of a registered letter, who nevertheless pays an .additional five cents in order to ensure safety.
Take my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue. With all due regard to his apparent innocence, I say that in my judgment he stands before me to-night as a Criminal. Two years ago, when he had been in office for six months, a young nurse at Kingston gave what she supposed to be patent medicine to one of the patients at the hospital. The bottle was wrongly labelled; instead of containing patent medicine, it contained poison, and the man died. The nurse was not responsible; she administered the medicine in good faith. The bottle was labelled as being regular patent medicine and was approved by the inspector of the Government. The inspector having been appointed by the Department of Inland Revenue and the appointment having been sanctioned by my hon. friend the minister, I say that he is a criminal, that he ought to be arrested and sent to jail as the causa causans. No minister, no poison. I always suspected, Sir, that there was some poisonous substance in the outfit, to use the favourite and courteous expression of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia. Last year the Bank Act was under consideration in the committee room upstairs, and at each and every meeting	I was pleased to
see my hon.	friend the minister,
in spite of his many duties elsewhere. We amended the Bank Act and made some new provisions. There ihad been a clamour in certain parts of the country that the Government should guarantee the deposits made in the banks and should be responsible, at all events, to the depositors. My hon. friend combatted that principle and I joined with him. I am conservative enough to stand for common sense. We have no paternalism in this country. We

must distinguish as between public institutions and private institutions, and banks are private institutions of a quasi-public nature. What did my hon. friend do ? What he did I am bound to say received my support in this House. My hon. friend agreed that the list of auditors should be submitted to the Department of Finance for its imprimatur, for its approval, before their appointment. That was a very wise piece of legislation. Some representatives of the people thought that did not go far enough. For myself I dare say that this was wise and sound legislation, and 1 heartily concurred in it. This is a sound principle, but does it obligate the Government to reimburse the depositors in case of errors of judgment on the part of its officers say, if auditors are appointed by them who are not qualified? No, Mr. Speaker. But I say that by the precedent he is creating to-day, by this legislation my hon. friend is taking a leap in the dark. There will be other errors of judgment, there will be other bank failures, especially if this Government is to remain two years more in office; and the depositors will come with a vengeance and say: If you had one justice for the province of Ontario you must have a similar justice for the other provinces of the Dominion. I say that as the Bank Act reads to-day there is no reimbursement provided by law. That is the language I held when I was appealed to-yes, and if I speak with some warmth upon this subject it is because I have been appealed to by my electors in the county of Eouville, where many orphans and widows were ruined by the failure of the Ville Marie bank. That is the language I held. I said to them: No, the Government does not reimburse depositors. That is what Mr. Fielding said when Mr. Monk, the late member for Jacques Cartier, appealed to him to obtain the reimbursement of the depositors of the banque Ville Marie. This is the language which I am sure the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce would have held if he had been the Minister of Finance when the Farmers Bank depositors appealed to my hon. friend. I am sorry the Minister of Finance was not in the House when his colleague the Postmaster General spoke this afternoon; did my hon. friend follow well what the Postmaster General said this afternoon ? The Postmaster General seized the weakness of the position taken by the Government in this case. He knows that in his own province depositors of the Banque du Peuple, the Banque Ville 
Marie and of the Banque St. Jean, and if there are survivors amongst the victims of the Mechanics Bank and other old institutions that failed in the past, he knows that they will appeal to him and that they will say: As you have paid depositors of the Farmers Bank who were the victims of fraud and recklessness on the part of Travers and his associates, so you will reimburse us who were victims of Bousquet of the Banque du Peuple, of Weir of the Banque Ville Marie. What did the Postmaster General promise? This afternoon he said in so many words that there had been no petitions, but that if they petitioned the Government, they would examine very closely their case. They would grant an investigation, and if it was proved that they were defrauded they would reimburse them as they now do with the Farmers Bank depositors. Did my hon. friend accept that principle as laid down by his colleague? Does he know that this will happen as sure as the sun will rise to-morrow morning? The Postmaster General asked; did the depositors of these defunct banks ever .appeal to the Government ? As he is new in this House I can forgive him his ignorance. As a matter of fact, in my knowledge, during the last seventeen years, I and other members have placed on the table of this House petitions from depositors in those three .banks; yes, many of the members on both sides of the House who. have been here since 1896 and before that have laid such petitions on the table. But what was the answer made by Mr. Fielding? What was his answer to our late colleague, Mr. Monk, when in 1900 Mr. Monk argued as my hon. friend, the Minister of Labour, argued this afternoon, as my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) will argue in a few moments, what was the answer made by the then Minister of Finance? He did not yield to pressure brought upon him by either his opponents or his own political friends. I myself approached Mr. Fielding and I said to him:	There has 'been fraud, there
has been recklessness in the administration oif the Banque Ville-Marie, the Government ought to reimburse the depositors. What was the answer made by Mr. Fielding, to all these requests? The Government was all powerful, it had a large majority behind it; everything was plain sailing. It was in the year 1900 and we were just fresh from a general election. Mr. Fielding answered as follows

' It is necessary to remember that a bank is only a private corporation doing business with the public. True, it is a corporation around which the Government throws more than the usual guards and checks and the public gets the benefit of these guards and cheeks; but surely it is not to be assumed that because an effort is made by the Government to ' throw around the banks additional guards and checks of unusual character, the Government becomes responsible for the whole business.' That was the attitude of a fearless statesman, of one who had the courage to stand in front of both friend and foe and to hold that dignified language. Mr. Speaker, the depositors of the Banque Ville Marie, of the Banque du Peuple, of the Banque St. Jean petitioned the Government and Mr. Fielding answered; No, this is not the business of the Government. Now with this legislation they can come again, they can again petition the Government. If you had read the petition I hold in my hand, Mr. Speaker, you would realize that its language is quite different from that of former years. The depositors now take their hint from the dangerous legislation, the perfidious, obnoxious legislation introduced by my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance. Three or four hundred people w'ere utterly ruined in my county by the failure of the bank Ville Marie, and they have signed this petition,:
We the undersigned depositors in La Banque Ville Marie pray you to present such legislation during this session of Parliament that we may be reimbursed of the deposits made by us in the said bank.
And, listen to this paragraph:
We believe that we are entitled to respectfully insist that this reimbursement should be made because of the legislation introduced by you reimbursing the depositors of the Farmers Bank.
Shall I read the names, Mr. Speaker, of the old and the young, of the widows and orphans, who were ruined in the county of Rouville by the mismanagement of La Banque Ville Marie-mismanagement which was known to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) when he was Finance Minister of Canada, as I shall prove in a minute?
What is the history of La Banque Ville-Marie? When t'he failure happened the bank had over 3,000 depositors, all farmers or labourers, in the district of Montreal. They were, as we say in French, belonging to la petite bourgeoisie. The bank was organized in 1874 with a capital of 300

$1,000,000. There were two issues of stock: the first for $<600,000, and the second for $400,000, which completed the $1,000,000. In 1881, the directors found it necessary to reduce the stock to half a million dollars, and even then all the shares were not held by bona fide stockholders. Though apparently the bank had that much paid up capital, it appears, and it is a fact, that only $300,000 was fully paid up. The failure of the bank was caused by clear dereliction of duty within and outside the bank, and, what is worse, the Government knew of the mismanagement during all those years. The late Mr. Monk, then member for Jacques Cartier, brought this matter up in the House, after having moved for a return of the correspondence and papers exchanged between the Department of Finance and the directors and officials of La Banque Ville Marie since January 1, 1890. The first letter, dated March 3, 1892, is addressed by
9 p.m. Mr. Courteney, then deputy Minister of Finance, to Robert Sedge-wick, K.C., deputy Minister of Justice, who later on became one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. I am sorry to weary the House by reading these letters, but I am making a case for the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie in my constituency. The letter reads as follows:
Sir,-I have the honour to call your attention to section 51 of the Bank Act, under which banks may issue notes for circulation to the extent of their unimpaired paid-up capital, and to say that the Banque Ville Marie has under the provisions of the Act issued notes varying since last July from $330,500 to $470,115. The bank makes a return of a subscribed capital of $500,000, and a paid-up capital of $479,250. The difference between the subscribed and paid-up capital appears from the return just received of shareholders of the bank on the 31st December last to be caused by the cancellations of shares on which no payments had been made and in a few cases from his shares not being fully paid up.
He adds that:
Thirty shares of this bank were sold on Monday last on the Montreal market at 85. I have therefore to ask whether, seeing the position of the bank as evidenced by this quotation and the fact that a great portion of its stock is held in suspense and in trust, the Government, under the Act, should take any action in the matter and if so in what direction. I shall be glad to be generally advised on the subject at your earliest convenience.
He then writes to Mr. Weir, the president of the bank, who answers that he is not well but will be in Ottawa in a few days, and will then explain. On the 29th July, Mr. Court-

ney writes to the Deputy Minister of Justice as follows:
Sir,-I have the honour to call your attention to my letter of the 3rd March last in reference to the position of the Bank Ville Marie, in which I ask to be informed whether in view of such position, the Government should under the Act take any action in the matter and in what direction. I have not yet received a reply to my letter of the 3rd March and I should be glad to be advised on the subject at your very earliest convenience.
Notice was given by the Deputy Minister of Finance that the bank was violating the law. Mr. Courtney writes to Mr. Weir on the 29th July as follows:
Sir,-I have the honour to call your attention to the fact that in the last returns from your bank the subscribed capital is stated at $370,500 in place of $500,000 in previous returns.
I beg also to call your attention to section 28 of the Bank Act which provides for reductions of capital stock only on approval of the Treasury Board, and as no such approval has been given, I shall be obliged if you will kindly explain your action in the matter. I shall be glad to hear from you at your earliest convenience.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: What year was that?

1892. The mismanagement of the bank was known to the old Conservative Administration, as I shall prove in a minute. Later on, Mr. Weir agrees to reduce the capital of the bank, and Mr. Courtney, the deputy minister, writes to Mr. Weir on the 2nd August, 1892, as follows:
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your letter of the 1st inst., respecting the reduction of the capital stock of your bank. I will have to make a report on the subject to the Minister of Finance, but as he is now absent from Ottawa X presume nothing will be done until after his return.
The affairs of the bank were going from bad to worse, and the state of affairs was known to the public. Mr. Courtney, in the following letter, dated September 21, 1892, gives notice of the mismanagement to the Finance Minister:
Hon. Geo.* E. Foster,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Foster,-I enclose a memo, respecting the Banque Ville Marie to which I beg to call your early and careful attention. Practically the bank has scarcely any capital and is trading on its note circulation and deposits. The Montreal Gazette quotes the stock as buyers 77J, sellers 90. I think the concern should be closed up.
This letter was dated the 21st of September, 1892, and the bank was allowed to continue its reckless existence until 1900 when thousands of people were ruined because there was no capital. Yet, Mr. Courtney, watch-
[Mr. Lemleux.j
dog of thb treasury, had notified Mr. Foster, then Minister of Finances. Mr. Courtney sends a memorandum; evidently he was somewhat nervous at the news he received every day about the condition of the bank; and the conclusion of- that memorandum, dated 21st September, 1892, read as follows:
The undersigned, in view of all the circumstances detailed above, begs to recommend that a special return be asked for from the bank, under section 86 of the Bank Act, and that in addition to the information suggested by the Deputy Minister of Justice, the hank he asked to give details of the item under the head of assets, '21 other assets not included under the foregoing heads'-the amount under this head being for the month of August last, $196,852.60, out of total assets amounting to $1,495,636.05.
With reference to the withdrawal of the Dominion Government account amounting to about $19,000, the undersigned recommends that the same be withdrawn and the account closed.
He also recommends that the bank be compelled to comply with the provisions of the Bank Act, and ask the Treasury Board for its sanction to reduce the capital stock.
Respectfully submitted,
J. M. Courtney, Deputy Minister of Finance.
Sir, was not the Minister of Finance of that day made aware of the mismanagement oif this, bank and of the fraud which was perpetrated? The deputy minister asked authority from the minister to close the bank, and he asked also that the Government deposit of $19,000 in the bank be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under what provision of
the Bank Act had the minister any power to close the bank or interfere with its management; iwhat authority under the Bank Act had he except to call for a special return, and where was the negligence?

My friend knows that there aTe ways that are dark and tricks that are mean, and a man can apparently be clothed with all the authority of law and be a pure scoundrel, as was the manager of the Ville Marie Bank. Mr. Weir presented returns every month, that appeared very clear and very honest, but notwithstanding all these returns Mr. Courtney knew what was taking place and he was advising his minister all the time to close the bank and withdraw the Government deposit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What authority was there to close the bank?
The authority of common sense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What provision was there in the Bank Act, enabling the minister to

interfere with the management of the bank? What could the minister do under the Act except to call for a special return.

The best answer I can
give to my hon. friend is that on receiving that letter the Minister of Finance gave orders to Mr. Courtney to withdraw the Government deposit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not closing the
bank.

Mr. Courtney said it
should be closed and Mr. Foster, then Minister of Finance, was expressly notified. Mr. Fielding was told by the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and by others, that there seemed to be something very strange about the organization of the Farmers Bank. Mr. Fielding's answer was that the provisional directors had complied with the law, as they had. Sir, if you pay the depositors in one ease, assigning as a reason that Mr. Fielding was forewarned, so must you pay the depositors in the case of the Ville Marie Bank because o:f negligence and error of judgment on the part of the then Minister of Finance in not closing the bank when so warned by his deputy. My hon. friend cannot get ou't of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no authority to close the bank.

If my hon. friend had, with respect to the Farmers Bank, a case against the Hon. Mr. Fielding as strong as the case presented here against the Minister of Finance in the Conservative Government in connection with the Ville Marie Bank, I would not speak this evening; I would be ashamed to mention the matter at all. But let us compare the two cases. Mr. Courtney notified Mr. Weir on the 22nd of September, 1892, as follows:
Sir,-X have the honour to inform you that I have duly submitted to the Minister of Finance the recent correspondence between ourselves relating: to the reduction of the capital stock of the Banque Ville Marie, and I am directed to inform you that the Minister of Finance is advised that the reduction of capital must be duly sanctioned by the Treasury Board under section 28 of the Banking Act.
I must ask you to take immediate steps to comply with the Act inasmuch as there is a time limit imposed in the section quoted.
J. M. Courtney.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where was there any negligence in that?

This letter says to the manager of the Ville Marie Bank:	You
must do something within a certain time,
and if you forego doing it you violate the 300i
law. Let us go a little farther, there is something still worse. Mr. Courtney writes to Mr. Weir on September 28, 1892:
Mr. Weir will immediately take steps to bring about a reduction of capital to $300,000.
Mind you, at that time the circulation of the bank exceeded1 the capital by something like $200,000.
He will reduce his circulation at once to that limit. He has promised to keep the assets in a shape to satisfy the Treasury Board. The Government balance to be reduced to $5,000, and not to be increased.
A fine institution that, which is not deemed strong enough to receive a deposit of $5,000 by the Government. The correspondence is a long series of notices and signal dangers.
Danger signals.

Yes, danger signals; I put the cart before the oxen, as the Minister of Finance has done in the case of the legislation now before us. Mr. Sedgewick, the Deputy Minister of Justice, on the 20th of October, 1892, answered the letter dated July, 1892. With all due respect to the memory of the late Justice Sedgewick, and he was a splendid man and an excellent judge and a gentleman of courtly manners, but as the Prime Minister knows, he was slow at times before answering letters. In October, 1892, Mr. Sedgewick, Deputy Minister of Justice, wrote to the secretary of the Finance Department:
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 18th instant, stating that prior to June last the Bank Ville Marie stated in its monthly returns that the subscribed capital was $500,000 and the paid-up capital $479,250, and that in the returns for June and subsequent months the subscribed capital was given at $370,500 and. the paid up capital at $350,000 ; and stating further that no application had been made to the Treasury Board for sanction of the by-law providing for the reduction of capital; and you ask three questions, which by direction of the Minister of Justice I beg to answer as follows:
(1)	Whether the reduction of the capital can be made without the sanction of the Treasury Board? A. It cannot.
(2)	Whether the by-law authorizing this reduction is absolutely void, or merely voidable as would seem to be the view of the legal advisers of the bank? A. The by-law in question was a mere step in the proceedings necessary under the ' Bank Act ' to lawfully make a reduction of the bank's capital. The by-law itself could have no operation until approved by the Treasury Board, but more than three months having elapsed since it was passed it is now absolutely void and inoperative for any purpose under section 28 of ' the Bank Act
In the opinion of the Minister of Justice, the advice given to the bank by its legal adviser, as stated in the president's letter of the

14th instant, cannot be supported, and the action of the bank in changing their books and making other returns as if the by-law had been approved is illegal.
(3)	Whether the officials of the bank, who sign the returns to the Government in the present shape are liable to the penalties prescribed under section 99 of 'The Bank Act?' A. From the facts as they appear in the papers they are not liable. The offence there specified is the making of any wilfully false or deceptive statements, whereas, the action of the bank officials in the present case appears to be rather the result of a mistaken opinion or judgment upon a matter of law upon which they have consulted their legal adviser.
(Sgd) Robert Sedgewick.
Deputy Minister of Justice.
This is all very tedious, yet illuminating at the same time, because we have there the evidence that the bank was violating the law; that the Government was advised of it; that the monthly statements were not made by the president of the bank. By this return I see that nearly every month the Deputy Minister of Finance had to wire Mr. Weir to send in his monthly statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was that negligence on the part of the Department of Finance? Was not the circulation, during the latter part of that particular year in question, in which he says: ' The consent of the Treasury Board was not obtained to the reduction in note circulation ' kept, as a matter of fact, within $350,000? I have information that it was. I should think the Deputy Minister of Finance was very diligent.
Yes, he was very diligent.	;

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then what are you complaining about?

Suppose that I was the president of the bank and that every month, owing to the violation of the law by me, my hon. friend was obliged to wire me to send in my monthly return? What would he think of me? Would he not have a vague suspicion that I was not only violating the law, but defrauding the public doing business with me? In answer to my hon. friend's second question as regards the circulation my hon. friend will get a Roland for an Oliver here because this is tne very gist of the case. As I stated a moment ago, it had been agreed that Mr. Weir should reduce the note circulation of the bank to the amount of the capital stock, which was $300,000. Let us see:
1893, month of July, circulation, $326,150.
Violation of the law.

August 31, circulation, $316,595.
Violation of the law.
September 30, circulation, $306,790.
Violation of the law.
October 31, circulation, $346,185.
Violation of the law.
November 30, circulation $320,070.
Violation of the law.
December 31.
Another violation of the law.
1894, September 30, circulation $339,390.
Another violation of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What was the paid-up
capital as reduced by the by-law in June, 1902? Was it not $350,000?
That does not appear by this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a fact.

Mr. Courtney does not say so. He complains all along that Mr. Weir goes beyond the capital stock of the bank, and 'besides Mr. Courtney forced Mr. Weir to explain some of the assets of the bank and to wipe them out. Mr. Weir, when arrested-I remember his trial, $nd the Postmaster General knows about it-was sent to jail precisely because he violated the law, by representing as assets what were liabilities-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where is the negligence on the part of Mr. Courtney?
There is no negligence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there is no negligence on the part of Mr. Courtney, my hon. friend's argument is absurd.

My hon. friend is making my case. I do not say that Mr. Courtney is guilty of negligence; but I say that if Mr. Courtney, during all those years, notified the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Foster, that Mr. Weir and the directors of La Banque Ville Marie, were violating the law, should not the Government be held responsible for the failure of that bank? You to-day hold the late Government as responsible for the failure of the Farmers Bank, because the certificate was issued by the Hon. Mr. Fielding. Well, of the two cases, if there is one where the Government should reimburse the depositors, I say it is the case of La Banque Ville Marie. I am not a populist; I am not a demagogue; I do not wish to defeat the provisions of the Bank Act. I voted with my

hon. friend last year, and I stood by him when he said that the Government should supervise the appointment of proper auditors; but when my hon. friend refused to listen to the appeals of my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and some other hon. members, who asked that the Government should guarantee the depositors against all losses, I stood against this proposition. Let my hon. friend understand me; I am still with him; but my hon. friend is without the law; I am within the law. My hon. friend ignores his own child. He wishes to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank, when he himself last year refused to amend the Bank Act in that direction. If my hon. friend reimburses the Farmers Bank depositors I protest against it. I say lit is not wise policy, it is a discrimination. If my hon. friend discriminates for the depositors in the Farmers Bank, he will do it for the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie.
