I represent them; as my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, as my hon. friend from North Ontario, as fifteen other hon. members on the other side of the House represent the depositors in the Farmers Bank. But if my hon. friend does not proceed with this legislation, I agree to return to my electors in Rouville and say: Gentlemen, I stand to-day where I stood many years ago when you urged us to make a pressure on Mr. Fielding and to get from him a reimbursement. Surely, Sir, there must .be one law for every province, and not one la.w for Ontario and another for Quebec. Equal justice, equal rights. My hon. friend knows the value of equal rights. I am an equal rightist. My hon. friend will not, I hope, surrender to the clamours of political gamesters, and I will undertake not to make any pressure upon this Government or upon any other government for the depositors of La Banque Ville Marie. But I say, if you do yield to the clamour of your political friends in order to secure some constituencies in Ontario, be fair, be just, and equally open the treasury to the poor depositors of the Ville Marie Bank, the widows and orphans who are in a similar or worst position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where is your negligence?
Mountains of evidence, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Absolutely no negligence
at -all.

For ten years the watchdog of the treasury, Mr. Cburtney, notified the then Minister of Finance that Mr. Weir was violating the law openly, in fact, he violated it every month in 1893 and 1894. The circulation of the bank exceeded the paid-up capital. What happened? The bank was doing no other business except to make hauls at the expense of depositors. A system was adopted by this bank of pilfering innocent, and in many cases ignorant people both in the country parts and in the city of Montreal. We find that by this confidence game it got -an immense -amount of money in places where you would not think it possible they could get so much. In fact, it was proven, when the case came before the court of King's Bench im Montreal, that Mir. Weir was giving increases of salary to the young bank clerks o.f his 'bank inasmuch as they would, increase the amount of deposits in their respective districts and decrease- the loans and the discount business of the bank. In Mais-on-neuve, for instance, they opened a branch in 1899; they took in deposits $17,000 and they only did a business of $12,000. In 1898 they opened a branch at Sit. Loui-s du Mile End, a suburb of Montreal; the deposits were $31,000, land only $4,000 of business; all the rest was sent into Montreal. At Ormstown, they opened -a branch in 1898, they had deposits of $30,000 and $8,000 of business. In May 1898. they opened a branch in Ch-aboillez Square, in the division of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). Here they made a tremendous haul; they got $44,500 in deposits, and did a business of $4,000, not enough to pay one smiall employee of the bank. But all this money was sent into the head office. At Marieville, in my county, a branch was opened in June, 1897; they had deposits of $70,000 and $4,000 of business. At Longueuil a branch was opened in 1897; they had $43,000 of deposits, $2,000 of business, and $41,000 was shipped into Montreal. At Chia-mbly, a branch was opened in December, 1896; they had $39,000 of deposits, and $9,000 of business. At Papineauville, in the county of Labelle, a branch was opened in 1896. They took $70,000 of deposits and did a business of only $10,000 of discounts. I know, as a matter of fact, that a very distinguished family, well known in this House, one of whose members was one of the most prominent members of this House, was practically ruined by the failure. In Nicolet they took nearly $70,000, and the discounts were $30,000. At L'Epiphanie they had deposits

to the extent of $98,000 and only $16,000 under discount. At Lachine, they had nearly $60,000 of deposits and $35,000 of business. At St. Laurent, Jacques Cartier county, the deposits were $65,000, and they did $35,000 business. That is the way the Ville Marie Bank managed its affairs with the knowledge of the Finance Minister of the day.
One fact which is very striking appears in one of the letters that Mr. Weir wrote, insisting on getting deposits from the Government.
The Farmers Bank did that too.

Yes, from the Ontario Government, through Mr. Beattie Nesbitt, who had many friends. Mr. Weir was a friend of the Government of the day. Under date of November 7, 1894, he says:
The reduction of our circulation will, of course, affect our earning power, and when, in addition to this, you reduce your deposit with us from the old average of $20,000, to about $5,000, you are placing us at a considerable disadvantage. I notice that the Hochelaga and Jacques Cartier Banks continue to hold an average of from $18,000 to $20,000 of your deposits, and I think the work we do is equal, at least to that of the former. At no time in the history of the bank has its position been equal to what it is to-day, and I cannot conceive why you should apparently discriminate against us.
And here is the typical answer of honest Mr. Courtney to Mr. Weir:
T have your letter of yesterday, in which, after treating of your note issue, you compare the balances due to the Government and held by the Hochelaga and Jacques Cartier Banks as against the balance held by the Ville Marie.
I presume depositors in controlling their bank balances take other matters into consideration besides the amount of work performed-in the case of the two banks to which you refer there is no shareholders' stock in suspense.
Does my hon. friend not see the irony of the Deputy Minister of Finance ? Mr. Weir is pleading and praying for larger Government deposits in his bank, and Mr. Courtney says: Well, my dear friend, ' depositors in controlling their bank balances take other matters into consideration besides the amount of work performed-in the case of the two banks to which you refer there is no shareholders' stock in suspense.' In other words, Mr. Foster was advised, if not. daily, at least weekly, by his faithful watchdog, honest Mr. Courtney, that this bank was mismanaged and was violating the law. Mr. Foster let matters drift and a few years afterwards the failure of the bank occurred, ruining, as I said, at

least three thousand depositors, not to speak of the bona fide shareholders. The duty of the Finance Minister of the day was to see that the law was carried out. In 1892 from sworn returns sent to the department, the bank was at fault.
Then, as regards the diminution of stock, the agreement with the Department of Finance had been violated, and the Government knew of its continuous violation. During that year the bank was dilatory in sending in its monthly statements. Letter after letter and telegram after telegram were sent to M(r. Weir, the president of the bank, from whom more or less lame excuses were always given. The quotations on the Montreal stock market showed that the shares of the bank when listed were sold at seventy-seven on the dollar; and finally none amongst the stock brokers would attempt to sell one of that bank's shares.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend suggest that that is just ground for closing the bank ?
iMr. LEMIEUX: Oh, no. But my hon.
friend has listened to what I have read before, and I appeal to him now, whether, if he had been Minister of Finance and had been told by Mr. Courtney that such conditions existed, the bank should have been closed? If Mr. Courtney had told my hon. friend that, according to the monthly statements of the president and directors of the bank, the circulation exceeded their paid-up capital, in violation of the law, would my hon. friend have maintained that institution? Would he not have followed the advice given by Mr. Courtney, closed the bank, if need be, or, at all events, have taken some drastic action to protect the public?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I affirm that under the law at that time, and under the law at the present time, the Government has not the power to close a bank; a bank can be put in liquidation only in one way, and that is in the manner prescribed in the Bank Act. I challenge my hon. friend to produce a provision which enables the Government to do otherwise.

Could not the Government have taken criminal proceedings when Mr. Weir was violating the Bank Act, when Mr. Foster had to withdraw the funds of the Government from the bank, and when Mr. Courtney was plainly telling Mr. Weir: You want to 'get our deposits, *but there are other considerations than

those adduced toy you in your report. We should close your bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not believe that there is a legal bank in Canada that had not, during the past ten years, permitted circulation at one time or other to exceed the limit prescribed by law.

False returns have never been allowed. No, Mr. Speaker, the duty of the Government was to see that the law was carried out as regards the stock issue and as regards circulation. My hon. friend is, I will not say too good a banker, but he is too interested a stockholder in reliable and safe banks not to believe that. He would not invest his money in a bank administered as the Ville Marie Bank was at that time. There is no question as to what the Minister of Finance would say if he were asked: Where will you put your personal savings, in La Banque Ville Marie, which Mr. Courtney denounced as violating the law, or in the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank, the Bank of Commerce, or in any of the other banking institutions which are operated according to the Bank Act? This was the contention of our late friend and colleague, Mr. Monk. In his opinion, the Attorney General should have taken proceedings against the bank for unobservance of the 'law. The bank might have been deprived of its charter by writ of scire facias. At all events, Sir, the Government should have investigated, and the public being thus warned the bank would have ceased to open branches in order to make the great hauls which it made on the savings of the poor people. When the bank failed1 the circulation was $515,000, and the bank redeemed over $200,000 of illegal circulation. It was proved that the bank manager speculated with the funds of the bank, and I am told this evening that there was nothing under the law to compel that bank to stop its illegalities, its mismanagement and its fraud. Sir, I am no demagogue; I am no populist; I say that I am satisfied with the law as it stands, with the safeguards and the protection that is provided by the Bank Act, which was promoted by my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance. I do say, however, to my hon. friend that he must have one law for al'l Canadians, not one law for one class of people and another law for another class. I repeat that this legislation is obnoxious and perfidious, and that it is condemned by the best minds not only
in the Liberal party but in the Conservative party as well. My hon. friend knows that and I challenge him once more to produce oefore this debate is over one single opinion of one single financier or 'banker of repute in Canada favouring this legislation. The hon. gentleman cannot do it; he cannot accept the challenge. Nay, more, I know as a fact that my hon. friend from the moment that he intimated that he would introduce this measure received letter after letter protesting against this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I desire to say to my hon. friend that I had not one single communication from anybody protesting against this legislation. Although I have not discussed the matter with more than one or two bankers, one of the most distinguished bankers in this country, a man who is at the head of one of the greatest institutions in Canada, has given his opinion that this Government is morally bound to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank.

Well, that banker- is
more of a Tory heeler than he is a banker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is not a Tory heeler; he occupies one of the most distinguished positions in the banking fraternity.
Is it a written opinion? It is not a written opinion, no banker would dare affix his signature to such an opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that I would ask the written opinion of anybody as to what legislation I should introduce into this House? This Government is quite confident, if I may be permitted to say so, to judge of the legislation which it introduced here without obtaining the opinion of bankers in the matter, no matter how eminent they may be.

I say that that one
opinion is the exception which proves tne rule. My hon. friend has received the opinion of one gentleman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And none against.

Let my hon. friend canvass the banking fraternity with regard to this matter. They are, under the control of my hon. friend; he is at the head of the banking interests ot this country; he is the fountain of all the finances of Canada. Has my hon. friend read the Montreal Gazette and the Star?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

The Montreal Gazette
says that this is obnoxious legislation; the financial press of this country condemns it. I point out again that my hon. friend will not find one banker of repute who will openly stand up for this legislation. He may receive the whispering opinion of a sycophant; some one may whisper to him: Mr. White, you are doing exceedingly, marvellously well; by the way. cannot you give some government deposits to my bank? I defy him, however, to get the opinion of Sir Edmund Byron Walker, of the Bank of Commerce, that of Sir William Taylor, of Mr. Meredith both of the Bank of Montreal, that of Mr. Angus, or that of the president of the Royal Bank in support of this Bill. I challenge my hon. friend to show that any of these distinguished financiers will ever say that the Government of Canada should on the one hand reimburse for political purposes some depositors in the province of Ontario while ignoring in Quebec the other unfortunate depositors who through fraud and recklessness, as in the present instance, have been deprived of their savings and have been ruined thereby.

This House has been in session upwards of five months and I have trespassed upon its time only for a couple of hours during the whole of the session; consequently 1 do not think that it is necessary for me to offer any apology to the House for occupying .a few moments in discussing this legislation, which is of importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I listened with a great deal of interest to the vehement and savage attack which the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) made upon this legislation.
Not savage.

ested, so I make no apology for discussing this legislation respecting the most appalling financial disaster in the province of Ontario -appalling not so much for the amount involved as for the great number of poor people engulfed in the disaster. Ruin and desolation and even hunger face many hundreds of these depositors, and the Minister of Finance and the Government ought to be commended for their action, founded as it is upon sufficient and justifiabje grounds, in bringing forward this legislation and implementing the policy of the Conservative party when in opposition. In my opinion, the responsibility for this loss to the depositors rests upon the shoulders primarily of one man, and one man alone, and that is the ex-Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding. The certificate was obtained by fraud. That, is found by Sir William R. Meredith. Notice that the fraud which was being perpetrated on the department was given to the exMinister of Finance, but he did nothing. I am not going to recapitulate the history of all the notices that were served upon the Minister of Finance as to the fraud that was being perpetrated on his department. Our esteemed and respected friend the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), the hon. member for West Toronto (Sir	Edmund	Osier),	SirEdward Clouston, and Mr. Leighton McCarthy, an ex-member of this House, sent warning after	warning	to
the department of the most serious nature saying that fraud was being perpetrated. It was proven that perjury had been committed by Travers, and had the minister followed up the notices he had received he would have seen that the warnings given him by these gentlemen were well founded. Not only did the ex-Minister of Finance receive notices before the certificate was issued, but shortly after the bank started operations he received confirmation of the previous warnings from Mr. Van-coughnet of the Farmers Bank at Milton. The letter which Mr. Vancoughnet wrote to the department is on file and confirms all the warnings that Mr. Fielding had received, and if the department was not satisfied with the notices it had received prior to the issue of the certificate, there should have been no hesitation whatever in accepting the letter of Mr. Vancoughnet, who was in the employ of the Farmers Bank and who gave facts within his own knowledge to the Department of Finance. Having received notice prior to and after the certificate had been issued, what was the duty 
of the department? Primarily, it was to see that the provisions of the Bank Act were carried out. The provisions of the Bank Act were violated entirely and the department should never have issued the certificate. AfteT the certificate had been issued it was the duty of the department to recall it upon receiving notices that the same had been, obtained by fraud and on that point I differ from Sir William Meredith, who finds that there: was no provision or power to recall the certificate. I think the arm of the law is sufficiently long to reach out and draw back a certificate that has been obtained by fraud, and in my opinion the Government of the day would have had no difficulty in issuing a writ and securing an order restraining Travers from acting upon the certificate. They should have refused the certificate in the first place, but, having granted it they should have withdrawn it. If they felt that they had no legal authority to withdraw the certificate, they should have had Travers arrested for perjury, thereby giving notice to the whole world that Travers was a perjurer and was not worthy of confidence, and then no business would have been transacted by the bank. The least they should have done was to warn the public against doing business with a bank manager who had obtained his certificate by fraud, but the Department of Finance was apparently paralyzed and could not act. It was speechless apparently, and could not warn the public in a matter of this kind. It gave this riotous concern authority to go out on its wild career to commit depredations in the rich agricultural sections of Ontario. Three men were primarily responsible for this, and if the veil could be withdrawn from the secrets that are hidden behind this whole transaction, if the light of day were thrown upon it, the disclosures would shock the whole Dominion of Canada. The late member for West Peterboro was one of the men primarily responsible for this disaster. Through the instrumentality of his loan company and his money Travers illegally made a deposit of $250,000. The next man that was responsible for this certificate being obtained was W. S. Calvert, then chief Libetal whip, and there was a very peculiar and significant intimacy between Calvert and Travers. The evidence shows conclusively that W. S. Calvert, who in influence and authority in this House was next to a Cabinet Minister, secured large loans from

Travers. The evidence shows that from $3,000 to $5,000 had been paid to somebody in Ottawa for securing this certificate. We all know that there was a cheque with a 'C' marked upon it. Mr. Travers seems to have mesmerized the chief Liberal whip on that occasion. We find that the intimacy was so great that in addition to lending him large sums of money, Travers offered Calvert a directorship in the bank. I do not know why Mr. Calvert should have been offered a directorship except that he was influential in the Liberal party and it might have been expected that if there was any difficulty in securing the certificate, he would use his influence, and it has been conclusively proved that his influence was used in that direction. Notwithstanding the repeated warnings to the department, Travers got his certificate clothing him with authority to transact the important business of banking in the province of Ontario.

It is only fair as Mr. Calvert was once a member of this House and is not a member now that we should defend him as far as we can. Where does the hon. member find the evidence 10 p.m. against Mr. Calvert that justifies him in the statements he has made?

I have hot the evidence. It is a peculiar and significant fact that any member who asks for a copy of the evidence cannot get it. I understood that a great many copies were ordered to be printed. I have sent up repeatedly to the Distribution office for a copy, but the evidence is so damaging that it seems to have mysteriously disappeared. I have only been able to get two copies so far.

I have read Mr. Calvert's evidence under the most severe cross-examination by the Government's lawyer, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to justify the charges made against him by the hon. member.

I do not, expect that Mr. Calvert admitted these things, because it would have most seriously reflected on him if he had. In addition to securing large loans through Mr. Travers from this defunct and bankrupt bank, which should never have been allowed to do business, Mr. Calvert wrote to the Customs Departs ment in Mr. Travers' favour, so that a magnificent yacht that was presented to Travers by some millionaire in Detroit was allowed to come in through the Canadian customs at one-tenth of its valuation. That
was another significant fact. Another significant fact is that Mr. Calvert, the Liberal party whip, takes it upon himself to suggest that the picture of Sir Wilfrid Laurier might be placed upon the bills of the Farmers Bank. I say that the intimacy between Mr. Calvert and Mr. Travers was most significant.
Did he get the consent of Sir James Whitney to put his picture on the bills?
I will read the letter if the hon. member has the curiosity to hear what it is?
Answer my question.

It would have been something of a political asset to the Liberal party, no doubt, if the picture of their leader had been placed on the bills of the Farmers Bank and scattered all over the Dominion. It was stated in this House, and it has been stated since, that Mr. Travers, because of the gratitude in his bosom for this certificate and for all the favours he received, made a large contribution to the $100,000 testimonal which the ex-Minister of Finance received. That has never been denied.
Where is the evidence of that?

Where is the contradiction of that fact? The hon. member for Algoma moved in this House that a list of the subscribers to the Fielding testimonial be placed on the table of the House, so that the public would know who subscribed, but that motion was voted down by the Liberals then in power.
There were three members of this House at the time primarily responsible for the issue of that illegal certificate, namely, the ex-member for West Peterborough, Mr. Stratton, the ex-member for West Middlesex, Mr. Calvert, chief whip of the Liberal party, and the Hon. Mr. Fielding, who granted it in face of all the warnings he received. I do not wish to impute any improper motives to Mr. Fielding, but I say that in view of all the suspicious circumstances the lid should be lifted off this whole transaction, and the full light of day let in. There is only one justification for this legislation, and that justification is to be found in the negligence and laches of tne Finance Department under Mr. Fielding. Any hon. member who votes for this Bill must vote in condemnation of the

Finance Department and of the ex-Minister of Finance. The member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross), the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and every other hon. gentleman who votes for this Bill must vote for it upon that ground and upon that ground alone. The members who support this legislation are not coming here asking for alms from this Government; we are not asking for mercy or for generosity for the sufferers, we are asking for mere justice on account of the negligence, the default, the delinquency of the ex-Minister of Finance and his department. The hon. gentlemen who votes for this Bill must vote in condemnation of the ex-Minister of Finance. You can sugar-coat the pill as you like, but that is the dose hon. gentlemen on the other side must swallow, who vote for this Bill. The hon. member for Middlesex swallowed the pill with a gulp and a grimace, and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) will ha/ve to do the same thing. I say that had the ex-Minister of Finance been alert and diligent in the discharge of his duties, there would have been no certificate issued to permit this man to go out on the highways and byways of the great province of Ontario and defraud the people out of thousands and thousands of dollars.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite have told us that they want some legal justification for this legislation and they have asked upon what legal grounds are we seeking restitution to the sufferers. I am not sure that the Liberal party, in its long history, nor yet the Conservative party, in voting money, have always acted strictly on legal grounds. But I have legal analogy for this legislation. There is the case of Ryiands vs. Fletcher, a leading case in, English law familiar to all lawyers, and that lays down the principle that where a man has a dangerous thing under his control and through his negligence he allows it to escape and it does damage to his neighbour, he is responsible for all consequential damages. If a man starts a fire on his premises, and through his negligence he allows the fire to escape and to do damage to the property of his neighbour, he is responsible for the damage done.

The case you cited was
a water case.

Yes, the defendant owned a reservoir, and through his negligence the reservoir broke and the water flooded the property of his neighbour, and the owner of the reservoir was held responsible. In

this case we had a dangerous man who could be controlled by the Finance Department, clothed by that department with authority to go out and do a banking business, when he never should have been allowed to do it, and on this legal analogy which I have cited the Finance Department is responsible for consequential damages. There is another case which affords legal analogy for this. I have in my hand a copy of the Washington Treaty of 1871, in connection with the Alabama claims, on account of which England had to pay $15,500,000.
Far-fetched.

I will read the finding of the arbitrators, and I do not think the hon. member will then say it is far-fetched. Everybody is familiar with the Alabama case in which England was found guilty of negligence in allowing the steamer Alabama to be equipped in her harbours and sail from them, after notice from the Government of the United States
This is the King's birthday, and it is a good day for a patriotic speech.

We have heard a great deal in this debate about what is the efficient cause, and what is the proximate cause, and what is the causa causans, but no person can draw sufficiently on his imagination to say that the proximate cause, or the efficient cause of damages in the Alabama affair was the equipment of the ship and the sailing of the ship from an English harbour. The proximate cause was the depredation that was committed by the Alabama when she got on the high seas.
The Alabama case is always regarded as bad international lav/.

The distinguished arbitrators who made the findings should scarcely be charged as being bad lawyers even by such an eminent and distinguished authority as the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie), who descended from the dizzy heights of a county court judgeship to become a member of this House.
Oh, what a fall!

With all due respect to the hon. member for North Cape Breton,
I would prefer the authority of the distinguished men who sat on the Alabama claims, to his. At all events England was held responsible by these arbitrators for allowing the Alabama to be fitted out in her harbours, and, after due

notice from the United States, to set sail. The fitting out of the ship was not the efficient cause or the proximate cause or the causa causans of the damage that was done to United States commerce. It was the depredation done by the ship after she got out of port on the high sea. That is identically the case here. Mr. Travers was a dangerous character, a man whose character and reputation was well known to the ex-Minister of Finance. He was clothed with authority in the shape of a bank certificate; he organized his bank, and he went through the province of Ontario, with the result that his bank failed on account of his mismanagement. Let me read part of the findings in the case of the Alabama:
And especially that it omitted-
That is, the British Government.
-notwithstanding the warnings and official representations made by the diplomatic agents of the United States during the construction of the said number 290, to take in due time any effective measures of prevention, and that those orders which it did give at last, for the detention of the vessel, were issued so late that their execution was not practicable;
And whereas, after the escape of that vessel, the measures taken for its pursuit and arrest were so imperfect as to lead to no result, and therefore cannot be considered sufficient to release Great Britain from the responsibility already incurred ;
And whereas the Government of Her Britannic Majesty cannot justify itself for a failure in due diligence on the plea of the insufficiency of the legal means of action which it possessed.
Four of the arbitrators for these reasons found against Great Britain, and Great Britain paid $15,000,000 in connection with these claims.
I would refer also to the debate in the British House of Commons in regard to this matter. I think that even the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) will not dispute such an eminent authority as John Stuart Mill. He was quite favourable to having this matter submitted to arbitration. On page 1194, under date of March 6, 1868, in the debate in the British House of Commons, John Stuart Mill made this observation:
It would have in fact to ascertain the real damage which the commerce of the United States had received from this act of negligence on our part in letting the Alabama leave our ports.
It was an act of negligence in allowing the ship to leave port. The fitting out of the ship was not the proximate cause of the damage done to United States commerce; it was the allowing of the ship to go out of port on the high sea.

Is it not
a fact that the court held that, because the Alabama was fitted out for what was in law an illegal purpose, she was held to be responsible for any damage she caused? In the case of Travers he was not fitted out for any illegal purpose, but for a legal purpose. The analogy does not hold good.

I presume that international law is founded not only upon equity and justice, but upon common sense, and we are asking that the question under discussion be treated in the same way. The Minister of Finance, knowing Mr. Travers' character, clothes him with authority to go throughout the province and do damage to a great many of the electors. Consequently the Government is morally responsible. Hon. members speak about legal responsibility. Every one knows that, no matter how negligent a minister may be in discharging the duties of his office, there is no legal liability.

I am sure the hon.
member is anxious to be fair. He made the statement that the certificate was given to Mr. Travers in spite of the evidence that he was a rascal. Where is that evidence?

Mr. Leighton McCarthy's letter. I have not had time to read it, but it has been read over and over again in this House. It sets out a list of six+een or seventeen frauds perpetrated upon the shareholders of the Farmers Bank. Those charges were verified by an affidavit of Mr. William Laidlaw, K.C., an eminent counsel of the city of Toronto. What further evidence would the minister require?
Referring to the debate in the British House of Commons, I want to point out what the late Right Hon. William E. Gladstone said:
The question of whether any what may fairly be called laches can be charged against us in the case, I take to be the very question which ' is to be referred.
Both John Stuart Mill and the Right Hon. William E. Gladstone were speaking in favour of referring this to arbitration, and saying it was wholly a question to be decided whether the Government had been negligent in allowing this vessel to be fitted out in her port and in allowing it to leave her port, after the United States had given notice that it should not be allowed to do so. The ex-Minister of Finance, however, knowing that Mr. Travers had perjured himself,

knowing that he had falsified his statements repeatedly, gave him, so to speak, letters of marque to go out upon the high seas of finance of the province of Ontario and secure deposits from amongst the poor people throughout the length and breadth of the land. This is an analogous case so far as liability is concerned; but in the case of a Government, we are not permitted to issue writs, we are not permitted to sue, and consequently we appear relying upon our just moral claims and upon the legal analogy of this case.
As I said before, the considerations which move governments are not always legal considerations. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) showed that the Liberal Government had paid out large sums of money at different times for worthy objects. There is plenty of justification for this legislation. We are appealing upon our rights, on the ground alone of the negligence of a responsible minister of the Crown in issuing a certificate to a notorious character, after having received notice that he was a notorious character. There is far more justification for us to pay these claims arising out of the negligence on the part of the Minister of Finance than for the Liberals to pay the losses in respect of the Quebec bridge. The Hon. Mr. Fielding, in reply to the hon. member for Hatton, some years ago, said:
In the judgment of the Government, it would he contrary to public policy to recoup the losses of any class of investors from the public treasury.
That was the ground upon wihich he based his refusal to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank. Were not these losses in respect to the Quebec bridge recouped? Who were the responsible men in connection with the Quebec Bridge Company? Political friends of the leader of the Opposition, for instance, the Hon. Mr. Parent, Prime Minister of the province of Quebec, mayor of Quebec, and chairman of the Transcontinental. These men had only invested some $15,400 in this enterprise, and the Liberal Government paid them, not only the money they had put into that enterprise, but the par value of their stock, $265,000, plus interest at 5 per cent to December, 1908, with ten per cent bonus on their money, after the institution was bankrupt, a total of $555,279. Is not that recouping the losses of investors in connection with private investments of this character? The Liberal Government paid to the Bank of Montreal interest on

the bank's loans and interest on interest in arrears, a total of $75,673. The total loss resulting to the country from the Liberal Government recouping the losses of their political friends was upwards of $7,000,000. The rich directors of the Quebec Bridge Company appealed to the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and his political friends, and got relief, but the poor farmers of the province of Ontario or any other farmers appealed in vain to the Liberal Government. The rich directors put $15,000 into an enterprise and take out $555,279, and they aie relieved' from their liability to pay up the balance due on their stock. Is not that recouping the losses of investors? Is that in consonance with the principle enunciated by the hon. ex-Minister of Finance when he gave his answer to the hon. member for Halton9 But, what was worse still, the Libera] Government paid back $300,000 of a subsidy to Quebec city. Was that paid back because Quebec city had invested in a speculative enterprise along with ex-Mayor Parent, Premier of Quebec, or was it paid back because the present leader of the Opposition was representing one of the constituencies in the city of Quebec? And they attack in a most vicious and savage manner a matter of $1,200,000, grounded as it is upon a just claim owing to the negligence of a responsible minister of the Government. It is more just to pay these claims than to have paid those caused by the loss of the Quebec bridge, or to have handed over millions of dollars in timber limits, grazing leases and water-powers to party favorites, or to have squandered $40,000,000 on the Transcontinental, or to have payed three-quarters of a million to political contractors like M. A good deal of controversy took place a year or two ago between Mr. Fielding and myself with regard to this matter. I came here on November 22, the day of the opening of the House in the year 1906; the certificate was granted to Mr. Travers on November 30. Between those dates, possibly not more than three days after I arrived in Ottawa, I went to Mr. Fielding and told him how the money was apparently being raised; told him that I had seen the notes in the hands of a solicitor; told him that I had seen the endorsements of the provincial directors upon those notes, presumably for the purpose of discounting. But Mr. Fielding made the assertion	that I
12 m. was mistaken. Well, I thought that my	memory
was just as good as that of the Hon. Mr. Fielding, and I still think so. I maintain that what I told the hon. gentleman was correct.	In discussing the matter in
March, 1911, Mr. Fielding repeatedly said that	I	was mistaken in the	statement
which I made -when I told the House that I went to the minister and acquainted him with the fact that I had seen those notes, and that it was my impression that certain things had taken place. During the course of his remarks Mr. Fielding said, 'the hon. gentleman is mistaken.' Later he said again, 'he is mistaken,' and at the end of a paragraph he says:
To the best of my recollection, he is entirely mistaken.
He was getting a little more emphatic every time. I want to submit a few facts to the House, and to ask hon. gentlemen who was in tlhe better position to judge as to whether ox not I was mistaken? I told the House that I came direct from a county in which a large amount of money had been subscribed in respect of this bank, and where I knew that there was going to be distress among the people if something was not done. I went to Mr. Fielding and had a conversation with him, feeling sure that I was correctly stating what took place. I had it vividly in mind at the time, and I gave as a reason why it was so vividly in my mind the fact that I was deeply impressed with the seriousness of the whole matter. In looking over 'Hansard' the other day, in order to find out just what Mr. Fielding said, I came across a letter from Mr. T.
C. Boville, the deputy minister, in which, addressing Mr. McCarthy, he said.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th instant, to Mr. Fielding's address respecting the Farmers Bank of Canada.
When application is made by the Farmers Bank to the Treasury Board for a certificate to enable them to commence business, the representations contained in your letter with its enclosure will be laid before the board.
The member for North Toronto, Mr. Foster, spoke on that occasion, and I intend to read a portion of his remarks in order to bring out prominently the point I wish to make: He said:
Bear in mind that on October the 23 rd the application was in-
That was the application for the certificate; the money was deposited on October 23.
-in the shape of a deposit of $250,000 to my own credit.
This is Mr. Fielding's statement:
Now, I will put this question to the hon. minister. From the 23rd October, 1906, until the 27th of November, 1906, will the minister say that either he or his department took any step whatever to convince themselves of the bona fides of this application or made any inquiry as to the standing or actions of the men behind it? That is a simple question, but there is a good deal in it. I will go further. The information which Mr. McCarthy gave was to go before the Treasury Board. Let me ask the minister if the Treasury Board met to consider this matter before the 30th of November, the very day when the certificate was granted. And I will ask him if he ever put before that board the information which Mr. McCarthy gave him, and which he declared would be put before them. That can be very simply answered.
I am going to read Mr. Fielding's answer, which, I think, settles the whole question as to whether Mr. Fielding's recollection or mine was the better. I stated emphatically that I had a complete recollection of the conversation. Mr. Fielding, his attention having been drawn to what occurred between the 23rd of October, 1906, and the 27th of November, 1906, with regard to placing information before the Treasury Board to enable them to decide whether the certificate should be granted, said:
I cannot remember what exactly happened between these dates.
He admits without hesitation that he cannot exactly remember just what took place between the 23rd of October and the 27th of November. If the gentleman could not remember what took place, why did he contradict me and say that I was mistaken when I stated that I went to him

between the 22nd and 30th of the month of Novemoer of that same year and informed him of the facts that I have mentioned, that these people were discounting notes in order to raise money instead of getting it from the source the Bank Act implied it should be obtained, namely the sale of stock. Mr. Fielding settled the whole question firms answer. I do not ask the House to take my word, I leave it entirely for Mr. Fielding to decide and he settles it surely. He says:
I cannot remember exactly what happened between these date3.
An admission of his inability to say whether I was right or not, and yet he said I was mistaken.
I shall look into the evidence for a few moments on this point. I have read a good deal of this evidence. I confess there is much in it that is confusing but, familiar as I am with many of these transactions, I feel that I am competent to trace out and gather up the truthfulness of the answers that were given. Here is a question put to Mr. Fielding when he was under oath, by the commissioner:
That would have occurred between the meeting of Parliament on the 22nd and the granting of the certificate on the 30th?
A reference to our meeting together and the conversation we had. He replied:
No, it probably occurred before that, X do not remember discussing with him the propriety of granting the certificate at all.
Remember, he told us before this that he did not remember what took place between the 23rd of October and the 27th of November and he repeats it on oath here:
I do not remember discussing with him the propriety of granting the certificate at all. My conversation would be bearing on the extension of the charter, the getting of subscriptions, the whole movement. The conversation I spoke of with Mr. Henderson would not have reference to the granting of certificates particularly.
Mr. Fielding immediately goes off woolgathering, he drifts away on to something that the commissioner did not ask him about, trying, as it were, to cover up and avoid a direct answer. He said:
Mr. Henderson never waited on me on the subject in his life.
A straight denial.
We met upon the Parliament grounds and occasionally had conversations.
When this occurence had taken place he seemed to mix things up so badly that for my part I would be utterly unable to gather his meaning. But we do come to a

point here where we can find what he was at. Mr. Fielding then said, continuing his answer to Sir William Meredith:
I think the day the certificate was granted I think I ran across Mr. Henderson and I said.
Now when he gets down right to the question that I had raised, the statement I had made, that 1 met him in the lobby cf the House of Commons a few days after the certificate had been granted and that he told me that Mr. Travers had been down and that he had questioned him with regard to the wlay the money was obtained and he had given him a certificate. Then this is what Mr. Fielding says on oath:
I think the day the certificate was granted I think I ran across Mr. Henderson and I said: Well, I have had to give these people their certificate and I am sorry for it.
Why was he sorry for it? I do not know but that settles tire point. Mr. Fielding admits that he ran across Mr. Henderson and that he told him that he had given these people the certificate and that he was sorry for it. Mir. Fielding had always denied what I said when I told the House and the country that I had a conversation with him in the lobby, and slaiid I was mistaken. He admits in the evidence that during the month from the 23rd of October to the 27th of November he did not exactly remember what took place. Now he says:
I think the day the certificate was granted.
We know what day that was, the 30th of November.
I think I ran across Mr. Henderson and I said: Well I have had to give these people their certificate and I am sorry for it.
I submit this question:	Why dad Mr. Fielding come to me and tell me that he had the interview that I had with him in November? He had denied that I approached him and told him about their discounting these notes but he would not give me credit for making that statement. Now I say why did Mr. Fielding come to me just after this certificate was issued and tell me what he had done? Why did he not go to you, Mr. Speaker, and tell you? Why did he not go to some other hon. gentleman in this House and tell him? Why did he not go to the Minister of Labour, whom he knew very well, and tell him what he had done? No, he came to myself and told me what he had done. Is there any hon. gentleman in this House who will

not conclude at once that Mr. Fielding came to me on account of the conversations we had had before this? That is why he came to me, it verifies the whole thing and removes !a doubt that I believe many people in this country had with regard to the difference of opinion between myself .and Mr. Fielding, and that is why I am making this statement. I think the evidence is complete and convincing. This evidence was repeated a little later on when Mr. Fielding was undergoing examination before the commissioner. Referring to the time the certificate was granted, he said:
What happened was that meeting Mr. Henderson that evening-I have no recollection of the part of the House-it was probably in the House-I told Mr. Henderson, 1 Well, I have given these people the certificate, or the Treasury Board has given these people the certificate, but I am sorry to do it.'
Repeating in another form the very same thing. Why did he come to me? why did he not go to somebody else? He no doubt came to me and made that statement because he had had a conversation with me the week before, when he had promised me that the certificate would be withheld as long as possible.
In my own interest, in self protection, I wanted to produce the evidence in this House to establish the fact that I had approached Mr. Fielding at a certain time, and had made a statement to him, -which of course he denied, I have produced this evidence to show that Mr. Fielding himself practically admitted that I was right and he was wrong. I regret very much to have to make this statement; I regret very much that I am obliged in my own self-defence to use the name of Mr. Fielding, with whom I was intimately -acquainted; but it is a duty which I owe *to myself and to this House, because, by *producing this evidence and showing exactly what took place, I think I have removed the doubt which possibly was in the minds of' a great many people, and which I was anxious to have removed.
The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition a few days ago referred to that portion of the speech of the Minister of Finance in which he referred to what he *termed the neglect of Mr. Fielding. I wish to make a brief reference to that. We often say that those who live in glass houses should never throw stones. There *was a very strong objection taken to the Minister of Finance speaking of Mr. Fielding's conduct as a matter of neglect. I cannot think it- was anything but neglect. I think that the hon. ex-minister neglected his duty; but the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition thought it was unfair in his absence to refer to his neglect. As I say, those who live in glass houses should not throw stones, but I have noticed in reading the evidence that Mr. Fielding did not hesitate to accuse me of neglect; and I thought if it was wrong on the part of the hon. Minister of Finance to speak of Mr. Fielding's actions as negligence, Mr. Fielding had no right to make a reference to my actions as negligence. Mr. Fielding tried to make a point against me by saying that I should have brought this matter up in Parliament, that I knew the facts, that I knew that this money was improperly obtained, and that I should have had the whole thing ventilated in the House. I do not know any reason why I should have brought it up any more than Mr. Fielding himself. He knew the facts as well as I did, he had his information from Mr. McCarthy, from Sir Edmund Osier, and from myself. We could not have primed him any more fully with information that this money was obtained -I shall say illegally, for the purpose of the deposit, because, notwithstanding the statement of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, the money was not obtained in the proper way. Mr. Fielding charges me with negligence because I did not bring the matter up in the House in order to have it discussed. The evidence shows that Mr. Fielding was asked the following question by the commissioner:
He-Mr. Henderson-had the information from Mr. Laidlaw which the department had previously to that?-A. If the department neglected its duty that was no reason why he should neglect his.
There is one other point that I wish to refer to. The question has often been asked, why I did not put my objections in writing. That was referred to only last evening. I said then that I did not believe there were five hon. gentlemen in this House who would have taken the responsibility of putting in writing the information I gave to Mr. Fielding at that time. It was critical, it was dangerous, for me to interfere. The information I conveyed to Mr. Fielding was for Mr. Fielding himself; it was not for the House of Commons or for the country; it was to put Mr. Fielding on his guard as chairman of the board that the money that was deposited was not obtained in the way it should have been, and that

consequently the transaction was illegal. Why should I be asked to write a letter and make a public display of something that was only intended for Mr. Fielding himself, or at the most for the board, who could obtain it from Mr. Fielding? As I said, it was not intended for the House, and it was not intended for the country, therefore I contend that I was perfectly justified in making my representations verbally, and that they were just as effectual as if they had been put in writing. Mr. Speaker, you know as I and every other member of the House knows, that we an have confidential conversations with ministers of the Crown on matters that we would never think of putting in writing. Sometimes it would be dangerous to put these matters in writing; it is not always proper to put them in writing. I know I have done this myself hundreds of times, and there is not an hon. gentleman in this House who has not gone to a minister of the Crown and presented to to him verbally certain facts that he wished to acquaint him with, and nobody ever thought that was a crime until this thing occurred, when, in order to make an excuse, they say: Why did not Mr. Henderson put this in writing? I think I have made my reason very plain indeed. Discussing this point the other day with one of the most active members on the other side of the House, he said that I was perfectly right, and that I could not have been expected to put my statement in writing and let it go on the files of the department.
Surely after twenty-six sessions in Parliament I have some limited knowledge as to how this sort of thing is done. I think ministers and ex-ministers will agree with me that these things are not always put on file and that there are many things that are better not put on the file. I base my answer on this, that the information I gave to Mr. Fielding was not intended for the House, nor for the country; it was for him to make use of confidentially when he came to issue the certificate, and it ought to have put him on his guard. What more could I do? If I had put it in writing no advantage would have been gained; Mr. Leighton McCarthy put 'his warning in writing, and it had no effect. It is said that Mr. McCarthy withdrew his information. He asked for the return of the papers, but he did not withdraw the information. The information which he conveyed to Mr. Fielding was left on Mr. Fielding's mind just the same as if Mr. McCarthy had never withdrawn the papers. If Mr. Mc-
Carthy presented his objections in writing and that had no avail, how would my objections have prevailed even if I had presented them in writing. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for the attention you have given.

After listening to the Minister of Finance and the other gentlemen opposite who have endeavoured to lay the blame on Mr. Fielding for the failure of the Farmers Bank, I cannot help thinking that they doth protest too much.	It struck me that the
Finance Minister when introducing the Bill was trying to atone for lack of facts and arguments by volume of words. At the time the certificate was issued the Bank Act said that certain things had to be done before the certificate could be issued,	and one of these
things was that the Minister of Finance was to be satisfied by affidavit or otherwise, that the deposit had been made, and the form of appointing directors gone through. The deposit receipt from the Bank of Montreal was in the hands of Mr. Fielding, the affidavits as to the bona fides of the subscription up to $500,000 were regular, so far as Mr. Fielding knew. The law says that the certificate ' may ' issue when the conditions are complied with, and ' may ' in this instance, I take it, means ' shall.' Mr. Fielding was asked for the certificate and he had no earthly right to refuse. He was simply acting in an administrative capacity and not in a legislative capacity. Bemember that this bank was conceived in iniquity. The name ' Farmers Bank ' was taken, so far as I can judge, for the purpose of deception. Mr. Fielding opposed an extension of time to acquire that certificate in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and that committee overruled him, as they should not have done, he being the Minister of Finance and head of the Finance Department. Since that time, the Banking and Commerce Committee have extended the time of charters for banks and other institutions, and they have done so this very session, when, in my judgment, they should not. If Mr. Fielding had refused that certificate there would have been a cry to high heaven throughout the land that he was standing in with the great moneyed corporations of Canada and refusing permission to the farmers to start a bank. I can imagine how the very men who have been loudest in condemnation of Mr. Fielding for the last couple of days would have shouted in condemnation of Mr. JUNE 3, 1914
Fielding had he refused to issue the Farmers Bank that certificate. These men who are so very loud in their condemnation and who are so very keen in their hindsight instead of in their foresight, would have been the very men to condemn Mr. Fielding if he had not issued the certificate. I do not agree that Mr. Fielding should not have issued the certificate and I do not agree with my hon. friend from Hatton that Mr. Fielding should have paid attention to the gossip that some one might pour into his ear in tihe lobbies of the House or in the walks around the grounds, especially when these people were afraid to put their gossip in writing. My hon. friend from Halton says there is no member in this House who has not gone to ministers and poured tales into their ears-, but he can look at me and see one member who never had any secrets with any minister, and who never had any tales to pour into their ears. Anything I have to say to a minister I am perfectly willing to put it in print and perfectly willing to stand on the floor of this House and repeat it, and that is what the hon. member for Halton should have done. I do not care who the busy man is, if you walk up the street and some fellow tells you some gossip, how long do you remember it? If I were to try to remember one-half the stuff that is told me verbally, I would go crazy in less than a week. The duty of a man who has anything worth while to report to a minister is to put it in writing before him, and he can easily mark it 'confidential,' and there is no man who would not trust Mr. Fielding to keep private any letter market 'confidential.' I am surprised at Sir Edmund Osier, who is a good business man, as everybody knows, prattling gossip that he was afraid to put in a letter to Mr. Fielding, and I can- say that for him, and to him so far as that is concerned. If Sir Edmund Osier knew anything that was wrong about the issuing of that certificate* it was his duty, as it was the duty of the hon. member for Halton, to put it before the Minister of Finance in writing and be prepared to stand by it. My hon. friend from Halton says he could not be expected to take the responsibility, but I say that, such being the case, the Minister of Finance had no right to take the responsibility on the say-so of the member for Halton, who was afraid to put his story in writing. Let me say that to my hon. friend.

It is not necessary; I appreciate what you say, but I do not think much of it.
Mr. NESBiITT: I do not care what you think; I am telling you what I think. When my hon. friend from Halton moved the resolution to which reference has been made, I said that I did not think the Government had any right to pay anything for any purpose outside of the ordinary expenditure of government, excepting perhaps on account of a calamity of some kind. I understand it was said by one hon. member to-night, when I was not present, that any one who voted for this measure voted against Mr. Fielding. If I thought that the people in my constituency would so construe a vote of mine in favour of this Bill, I certainly would vote against it. I do not believe, however, that the people in my constituency will think, even if I do vote for the Bill, that it is because Mr. Fielding was negligent or did not attend to his duties properly.
In the election of 1911, my right hon. friend the Premier and the Minister of Trade and Commerce attended a meeting in the town of Woodstock. I do not say that the Premier or the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave my opponent the authority; but the people in my constituency, who were vitally interested in this, told me after the meeting that he had said that, if the Conservative party were returned to power, they would repay the depositors in the Farmers Bank. Not one, not two, but several persons told me that my opponent went through the municipalities in the riding I have the honour to represent affected by the Farmers Bank, making that statement. I was, therefore, placed in rather an awkward position; but I followed my usual policy, and told my constituents frankly that I did not think any government had any more right to repay the depositors in the Farmers Bank than to repay the losses of any man engaged in any business. I fought the campaign on that basis. I told my constituents that frankly at all meetings, in places where the people were affected by the failure of the Farmers Bank. Several of the people in my constituency were at the meeting at Ingersoll, which the present Minister of Labour addressed. I was in the riding the next day, and they told me that he had said positively that, if the Conservative party were returned to power, they would repay the depositors in the Farmers

Bank. I told my constituents at the meeting at Kemptville, and the next night at the meeting at Kintore, that I did not think the Government had any right to repay the depositors, and that I could not make any promise that they would do so. Therefore, if I vote for this Bill, it is not because it is necessary for me to do so on account of the electors in my section of the country, because I have fought out this question with them before. In my constituency, however, the latter president of the Farmers Bank happened to be a gentleman who was the height of honour and integrity, namely, Colonel Munro, a man who represented that constituency for two parliaments in the Ontario House, a man who was not only highly respected but absolutely beloved by the people in that district. The fact that this bank that was conceived in iniquity seduced my friend Colonel Munro to be president of it, was the reason of the enormous deposits in my constituency. It was on account of the faith of the people in Colonel Munro that made them deposit their money with him. Some few of them might have been induced to make deposits on account of additional interest that the Farmers Bank was paying over and above what the other chartered banks were paying. A good many people in that section of the country thought, and still think, so far as I know, that any bank chartered by the Dominion Government is guaranteed by the Dominion Government. I found in the election campaign of 1911 that it was almost impossible to take out of the minds of the people the idea that a chartered bank is guaranteed by the Government. Since the election of 1911, this has become in my section of the country a public calamity. There have been three deaths directly traceable to the losses in this bank. I had a letter just the other day from an old lady, ninety years of age, whose husband is the same age. They cannot work; they had all their money deposited with Colonel Munro, and they are built up, like a great many others in my constituency, with the promises of my hon. friends and with the hopes held out by my hon. friends that they will repay these deposits; and Heaven only knows what will happen more than has already happened if this Bill does not go through. Therefore, I have a duty to perform to the people whom I represent.
I am sorry that so much has been said in trying to throw the blame of the failure of the Farmers Bank on the Hon. W. S.
Fielding. Man after man on the opposite side of the House has said that, if this certificate had not been issued, the bank could not have failed. If the sun did not shine, we could not have daylight. What an absurd thing to say. iEvery one knows that, if the certificate had not been issued, the bank could not have been organized, and it certainly could not have failed. The thing is so absurd and ridiculous that I am surprised .any human being, who has grown to manhood or babyhood, would make such a statement; but .my hon. friends have done so. If the certificate had not been issued, the bank certainly could not have failed, simply because it could not have started. I will not detain the House any longer, but I shall be forced, I am *afraid, to vote for this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to make
a few remarks in regard to the Bill now before the House. The riding that I represent has suffered a considerable loss through the failure of this bank. In the county of Oxford, I believe, there was on deposit at the time of the failure $148,622. The bulk of that deposit w.a3, however, in the north riding, represented by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat.
I want to take issue with the argument advanced by the last speaker, thlat no blame can be .attached to the late Minister of Finance for issuing the certificate to this hank. It is not necessary to refer to the report of the commissioner, who makes it quite clear that that is not the case. This matter liais been referred to by so many speakers that I would not mention it now were it not for the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for North Oxford. The commissioner says:
It is true that, as Mr. Fielding stated in evidence, Travers, so far as he knew, was a reputable hanker; but that was not, in my opinion, a sufficient reason for not having instituted an inquiry as to the matters which had been called to his attention. Such an inquiry could easily have been made, and the delay occasioned by it would have been inconsiderable, and such an inquiry would, undoubtedly, have resulted in the discovery of the manner in which the $100,000 had been raised and in the refusal of the Treasury Board to give the certificate.
That is so clear that I do not think it is necessary to make any further reference to it. The Minister of Finance was negligent in not properly discharging his duty and protecting the people, he being the trustee in that respect upon that occasion.

Now, I want to be very brief, and I am not going to deal with many things that otherwise I would like to have touched upon. But when an hon. gentleman gets up in this House and charges the Minister of (Labour with having made statements at Ingersoll in the riding I represent, a charge that has been repeatedly made by hon. gentlemen opposite and circulated by the Liberal press, and which has been repeatedly denied-I want to say here and now that in so far as my constituency is concerned he addressed no political meeting in the town of Ingersoll during the campaign of 1911. Yet he is charged here by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) with having said that if the Conservative party were returned to power they would reimburse the depositors in the Farmers Bank. That is the kind of argument repeatedly advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite during this debate. They cannot possibly get away with a statement of that kind. I repeat again that the Minister of Labour did not address a political meeting in Ingersoll during that cam-ipaingn.
I want to state also, with reference to the attack made on the hon. member for Halton, that the commissioner also says that it was not material whether that hon. gentleman's objection was a verbal one or a formal one. It is claimed that the commissioner did not condemn the late Administration as severely as hon. gentlemen on this side contend, but the commissioner says that the verbal report of the hon. member for Halton was just as effective as if it had been put in writing, and was what one would naturally expect between two members of this House, well known to each other, with a mutual high regard. I think that is what gentlemen so situated would naturally do.
Reference has been made by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) to fourteen or fifteen constituencies that were influenced in the last election by the Farmers Bank issue, but the insinuation has been made that there are members in this House who would not have been here had it not been for the promises they made in connection with this matter. I want to say that in so far as I am concerned-and possibly some of them may have had in mind the constituency I represent, as I happen to be the first Conservative ever elected from that constituency, -I made no promise nor pledge regarding this matter. I discussed it on several 302
occasions and pointed out where I thought the late Government and the Treasury Board were negligent, but in so far as making a pledge or promise is concerned I did nothing of the kind. I may say that the hon. member for the North riding (Mr. Nesbitt) took a different attitude. He claims that the Minister of Labour did these things in the South riding at Inger-sull and that he made use of them in his own riding. I may say that I admire consistency, and the old saying is true: consistency thou art a rare jewel, and his lack of consistency is apparent when you compare the statements he made here to-night with those he made in 1911, when he opposed the appointment of a commissioner to investigate the charges then made that there had been negligence by the Treasury Board. I am just going to *make a reference or two to hie statements upon that occasion. He said:
I also have a large number of people in the riding that I have the honour of representing in this House who have been severely punished.
We all know that when a person is punished it is for committing an offence. What was the offence these sufferers in that constituency, who had lost $106,000 had committed? They had not deposited their money in the Post Office Savings Bank, but had put it instead in a bank that had been incorporated by Act of Parliament and which had received a certificate to do business from the Government of Canada. Yet the hon. gentleman says they have been punished for not depositing their money in the Post Office Savings Bank. And a little further on in the debate, he says:
Nobody sympathizes with these losers more than I do, but I do not see why we should be asked to take money out of the public treasury to reimburse them. They deposited their money in the Farmers'Bank with their eyes wide open, when they had, as I have said, other places where they could have deposited it with absolute safety, guaranteed by the Government itself.
Who said that?

The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in a debate in this House.
Mr. NESBITT; I told them that on the platform.

I am just coming to that. The statement has been made that the Farmers Bank question exercised a great influence in electing certain members to this House at the last election. I want to point out that in the election of



1906 the hon. member for North Oxford had a majority of 124 and. in 1911 his majority wae increased to 295. You do not find that the people were swayed very much by the arguments upon that occasion. In 1908 I was defeated by 93 votes, and in 1911 I was elected by a majority of 24, not a very great change. I made no use of these arguments; I believe that there are very few members in this House, ae the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) has pointed out, as a result of any influence exerted by the Farmers Bank question.. And I believe that is a fact in the county from which I come. There was an issue that overshadowed every other so far as people of that county were concerned and that was reciprocity.
I am not going to take up the time of the House any further. I wish to state, however, that I am glad to have an opportunity of placing myself on record here to-night to show where I stand with regard to the people who have suffered through the lack of attention-or if I am not permitted to use a harsher term,- through the failure of the trustee to see that the management of this bank were not permitted to defraud the people of Canada to the extent to which they were defrauded. This bank should never have been permitted to be incorporated under the name The Farmers Bank of Canada unless there was an absolute guarantee that they would carry out the business which they claimed it was their intention to carry out. They established branches in small places throughout the country where there were no banks and in this way endeavoured to lead the farmers of the various counties to believe that their institution was to be for the benefit of the farmers. It was well known in the industrial centres and I believe that it was well known by the Banker's Association before the collapse came that the Farmers .Bank was in a most deplorable. condition. It will be observed that very little or no money was lost by the depositors in the towns and cities; the greatest losses were sustained by depositors in small places who had been led to believe that this institution was for their own special benefit.
I shall have the greatest pleasure in supporting this measure. I do not know that I would have spoken at this late hour had it not 'been for the deliberate attempt on the part of the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) to misrepresent the attitude of the hon. Minister of Labour, whose

arguments in defence of this measure are, unanswerable. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk in a general way around the subject, but I have failed to observe any arguments put up by them which successfully answered those advanced by the Minister of Labour.
Permit me to conclude by saying that in the few remarks which I have made I have attempted to discharge the duty that I owe to the people of my constituency, which I feel I would owe to them in the same measure if not a dollar had been deposited in this bank by persons in my county.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North):
speechtext:
The facts in connection with the very important measure that is now before the House have been dealt with at considerable length, and I would not undertake to address you, Sir, were it not 'for the fact that I hold very strong views upon this subject, and	that	I do not careto pass a	silent vote	upon a
question involving such far-reaching principles as are involved in the one now under consideration.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sutherland) addressed himself to the circumstances surrounding the failure of the Farmers Bank in his own
1 a. m. riding. I have no particular objection to take to anything which the hon. gentleman said. I have the greatest sympathy with any hon. member who represents electors who were unfavourably affected by the failure of this bank. I am not going to make any assertion as to what my attitude might possibly be if some of my constituents were similarly circumstanced ; but whatever my position might be, I do not for a moment contend that any change of attitude from the one which I now propose to take would he justified by the law or by the facts here presented.
I submit that public moneys should be used in the interest of the public; I make that statement boldly and broadly. We are here as a public body, as the highest court in this land, to deal with the money of the people and to deal with it in a manner that will be for the advantage of the country at large. No matter how sympathetic we may be in respect of the peonle who met with losses by reason of this failure, I submit that the way to remedy or remove the difficulty which has arisen is by the use of our private fortunes and not by giving away moneys which do not belong to us. If any person wants to be a philanthropist, he has a perfect right to carry out his philanthropic ideas by the use of his own private means;

but the carrying out of his philanthrophy by using the money of other people when he has no warrant or authority for doing so is a different matter. There is an old story, related, I think, by Mark Twain, that an enterprising gentleman once said that he was willing on certain occasions to sacrifice all his wife s relations for certain purposes. It is, perhaps, an easy matter for one to sacrifice, without any twinge of conscience, his wife s relatione, 'and it is, perhaps, easy for some persons to be generous with other people's money. One of the chief objections I have to this legislation is that we are applying public moneys to private pur-[DOT] poses and there is no justification whatever for such application.
It has been said that because we on this side of the House venture to express our opposition to this measure, we do not sympathize with the people who lost their money. We can not always carry out our sympathies in matters of this bind. There are public duties which men have to perform and which they carry out irrespective of whether or not their private sympathies are in line with their action. Speaking for myself, if this legislation, were a mere matter of sympathy, a mere matter of helping out the people who lost money through the failure of the Farmers Bank, I should be very glad to support it; but this legislation is establishing a dangerous policy which cannot by any possibility be universally applied, and that being the case, I cannot vote for it.
Something has been igaid by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) about an attack made upon him by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). It is a new experience that the hon. member for Halifax should be charged with having made an attack upon anybody. The hon. gentleman has been in this House for quite a number of years, and I really thought that his weaknesses were in the other direction ; that if an attack were really necessary the hon. member for Halifax was the last man who should be chosen to make it.
I listened to his speech last night and heard all he said in reference to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), and I am pleased to say I cannot find anything in it which would in any way constitute an attack upon the conduct or otherwise of that hon. gentleman. It is true that the junior member for Halifax said that the hon. member for Halton was the author of this trouble which this country is put to in regard to the Farmers Bank. It is 302i
perfectly true that this political agitation which was started in this House some four years ago was started by the hon. member for Halton. It is true and he has stated himself that he did not formulate the shape in which that attack was to be made that he was simply the spokesman of the party; that is what he says, and that he carried forward their views. There is no person on this side who was supporting Hon. Mr. Fielding's party at the time who has any doubt as to what was the purpose of that attack. That attack was made for political purposes; in the first instance to make a political attack on Mr. Fielding who was a strong man in his party. It was hoped that by making this attack on him, by impugning his capacity and integrity as a minister of the Crown he would be weakened in the country generally. That was one of the reasons; the other was the holding out of a bribe generally to the many people in Ontario and elsewhere who were involved and who had lost their money. Therefore there was a double purpose and thait purpose is carried on to the present day. The attack upon the late Minister of Finance is not now 'So strong before the minds of hon. gentlemen as they confess. This matter is now on a bribery basis.
